Benchmark.title: CIS CockroachDB v25.x Benchmark
Benchmark.description: All CIS Benchmarks ™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to maintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be used in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: • Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and quickly updating with the latest security patches. • End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), etc.). • Logging and monitoring user and system activity. In the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity program. Important Usage Information All Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They can be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of manual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with assessment: • CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT ® Pro Assessor) • CIS Benchmarks ™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling These tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of systems and applications. NOTE: Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can be fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL Recommendations ( Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are important for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for audits. Key Stakeholders Cybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative within an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and efficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration guidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions to specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the problematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. These exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing purposes. Apply the Correct Version of a Benchmark Benchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and applying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to be incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target systems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed: • Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the environment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of Benchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and Stand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. Applying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. • Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, but especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently and using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for auditing and remediation. Exceptions The guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not requirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The Benchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, with known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the Impact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific requirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a Recommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend that a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system's primary purpose is to function as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this Recommendation for that specific server). In the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and acceptable, and should be handled as follows: • The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well documented for audit purposes. • A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the future, if applicable. • If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward mitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. It is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and which settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for the organization. Remediation CIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of hardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark's “Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make that Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. When remediating systems (changing configuration settings on deployed systems as per the Benchmark's Recommendations), please approach this with caution and test thoroughly. The following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: • CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be applied to production systems without proper testing. • Proper testing consists of the following: o Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted systems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations (e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). o Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if there might be an issue with the targeted systems. o Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues arise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production systems. o When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production systems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be resolved prior to deploying more broadly. o When the initial deployment above is completed successfully, iteratively deploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this process until the full deployment is complete. Summary Using the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being selective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible to harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe manner. NOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks ™ are available for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats of the CIS Benchmarks ™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for CIS SecureSuite ® members. CIS-CAT ® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite ® members. Target Technology Details This document, CockroachDB Benchmark, provides prescriptive guidance for establishing a secure configuration posture for CockroachDB. This guide was tested against CockroachDB version 25.x running on Ubuntu Linux, but applies to other Linux distributions as well. To obtain the latest version of this guide, please visit http://benchmarks.cisecurity.org. If you have questions, comments, or have identified ways to improve this guide, please write us at feedback@cisecurity.org.

Rule.title: Obtain the binary from an official and trusted source and verify the SHA-256 sum after downloading.
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB server binaries and supporting tools must be obtained only from official Cockroach Labs release sources and verified using the published SHA-256 checksum before installation. The canonical sources for CockroachDB self-hosted binaries are: • The CockroachDB Releases pages, which link to official versioned binaries. • https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/ (binary distribution site), which hosts release artifacts such as full binaries and associated checksum files. For FIPS-ready runtimes, Cockroach Labs publishes per-version download links and corresponding SHA-256 checksum files (e.g., cockroach-v25.4.0.linux-amd64- fips.tgz and cockroach-v25.4.0.linux-amd64-fips.tgz.sha256sum) on the official documentation site and serves them from binaries.cockroachdb.com. Administrators must verify that the locally computed SHA-256 checksum of any downloaded CockroachDB binary matches the corresponding checksum value published by Cockroach Labs before using it for installation or upgrade.
Rationale: Obtaining CockroachDB binaries exclusively from official Cockroach Labs distribution endpoints and verifying them against the published SHA-256 checksums helps ensure: • Integrity - The downloaded binary has not been corrupted or altered in transit. • Authenticity - The binary corresponds to an official Cockroach Labs release and is traceable to a documented version. • Consistency - All CockroachDB nodes and environments run binaries that match known, documented release builds. Relying on unofficial sources or skipping checksum verification increases the risk of: • Malicious or trojanized CockroachDB binaries. • Outdated builds with known vulnerabilities. • Inconsistent behavior between environments due to untracked or modified binaries.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Reconfigure package pipelines Update all package managers, automation scripts, and manual runbooks to download CockroachDB binaries and tools only from: • https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/, or • A vetted internal mirror that pulls from this official source. 2. Download CockroachDB from official source and verify checksum #Example: Linux ARM64; Adjust VERSION as needed VERSION="v25.3.4" wget "https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/cockroach-${VERSION}.linux-amd64.tgz" # for Linux x86_64 use "https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/cockroach- ${VERSION}.linux-amd64.tgz" wget "https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/cockroach-${VERSION}.linux- amd64.tgz.sha256sum" # for Linux x86_64 use "https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/cockroach-${VERSION}.linux- amd64.tgz.sha256sum" # Verify checksum sha256sum "cockroach-${VERSION}.linux-amd64.tgz" cat "cockroach-${VERSION}.linux-amd64.tgz.sha256sum"

check.check-content: 1. Inspect package pipelines / automation Review CI/CD pipelines, configuration-management code, and installation scripts that fetch CockroachDB binaries. Confirm they download CockroachDB artifacts only from: • https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/, or • An internal mirror that itself synchronizes exclusively from Cockroach Labs official distribution. Inspect your package pipelines to ensure they only pull from binaries.cockroachdb.com. 2. Verify checksum for a downloaded artifact On an administrator workstation or build node: #Example: Linux ARM64; adjust FILE_NAME/VERSION as needed VERSION="v25.3.4" FILE_NAME="cockroach-${VERSION}.linux-arm64.tgz" # for Linux x86_64 use "cockroach-${VERSION}.linux-amd64.tgz" FILE_URL="https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/${FILE_NAME}" SHA_URL="${FILE_URL}.sha256sum" # Ensure file exists locally (or download it) if [ ! -f "$FILE_NAME" ]; then echo "Missing $FILE_NAME. Download it from official source first: $FILE_URL" exit 1 fi # Verify SHA-256 checksum against Cockroach Labs-published value if [ "$(wget -qO- "$SHA_URL" | awk '{print $1}')" == "$(sha256sum "$FILE_NAME" | awk '{print $1}')" ]; then echo "OK: SHA-256 matches Cockroach Labs' published checksum." else echo "FAIL: SHA-256 mismatch. File may be corrupted or tampered." exit 2 fi If the checksum does not match the published SHA-256 from Cockroach Labs, this is a finding. Expected Results: • All automation and manual procedures that obtain CockroachDB binaries: o Pull artifacts from https://binaries.cockroachdb.com/ or from an internal mirror that itself only syncs from Cockroach Labs official sources. • For each CockroachDB binary used in production or non-production environments: o The SHA-256 checksum is verified against the corresponding Cockroach Labs-published.sha256sum before installation or upgrade. • Any mismatch between the computed checksum and the published checksum is treated as a security finding, and the affected artifact is not used.

Rule.title: Ensure CockroachDB systemd Service Files Are Enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Confirm, and correct if necessary, that the CockroachDB systemd service is enabled on Linux-based systems. This ensures CockroachDB starts automatically at system boot, recovers gracefully from crashes, and is consistently managed under a dedicated non-root service account.
Rationale: Running CockroachDB as a foreground/background process without a service manager increases the risk of: • Nodes not starting after system reboot or crash. • Inconsistent privilege separation (e.g., accidentally running as root). • Logs not being integrated into the system audit/logging pipeline. By enabling CockroachDB as a systemd service: • The service is automatically started at boot and restarted on failure. • CockroachDB runs as a dedicated non-root account (cockroach), enforcing least privilege. • Service lifecycle is auditable via systemctl.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: For each initial node of your cluster, complete the following steps: 1. Create the Cockroach directory: mkdir /var/lib/cockroach 2. Create a Unix user named cockroach: useradd cockroach 3. Move the certs directory to the cockroach directory: mv certs /var/lib/cockroach/ 4. Change the ownership of the cockroach directory to the user cockroach: chown -R cockroach /var/lib/cockroach 5. Download the sample configuration template and save the file in the /etc/systemd/system/ directory: curl -o cockroach.service https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cockroachdb/docs/main/src/current/_includes /v25.4/prod-deployment/securecockroachdb.service OR [Unit] Description=Cockroach Database cluster node Requires=network.target [Service] Type=notify WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/cockroach ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cockroach start --certs-dir=certs --advertise- addr=<node-address> --listen-addr=<node-address>:26357 --sql-adr=<node-address>:26257 --http-addr=<node-address>:8080 -- join=<node1 address>,<node2 address>,<node3 address> --cache=.25 --max-sql- memory=.25 ExecStop=/usr/local/bin/cockroach node drain --self --certs-dir=certs TimeoutStopSec=300 Restart=always RestartSec=10 StandardOutput=syslog StandardError=syslog SyslogIdentifier=cockroach User=cockroach [Install] WantedBy=default.target Save the file in the /etc/systemd/system/directory. 6. Customize the sample configuration template for your deployment: Specify values for the following flags in the sample configuration template: • --advertise-addr: o Specifies the IP address/hostname and port to tell other nodes to use. The port number can be omitted, in which case it defaults to 26257. o This value must route to an IP address the node is listening on (with -- listen-addr unspecified, the node listens on all IP addresses). o In some networking scenarios, you may need to use --advertise-addr and/or --listen-addr differently. For enhanced security, it is a best practice to separate the listen address for inter-node communication from the listen address used for client SQL connections. • --join: Identifies the address of 3-5 of the initial nodes of the cluster. These addresses should match the addresses that the target nodes are advertising.. • Optionally include --locality: if using multi-region/latency-aware features. 7. Reload systemd and enable the service: systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable cockroach.service systemctl start cockroach.service Repeat these steps for each additional node that you want in your cluster. Note: systemd handles node restarts in case of node failure. To stop a node without systemd restarting it, run : systemctl stop cockroach.service

check.check-content: Run the following to confirm that CockroachDB is registered as a systemd service and enabled: ## Identify CockroachDB service unit if it exists systemctl list-unit-files | grep cockroach | awk '{print $1}' # Check if the service is enabled at boot systemctl is-enabled cockroach.service (or as identified from previous command) # Confirm it is active and running systemctl status cockroach.service # Verify it runs under the dedicated 'cockroach' user ps -u cockroach -f | grep cockroach Expected Results: • A CockroachDB service unit (for example, cockroach.service or securecockroachdb.service) exists under systemd. • The unit is enabled and active (running). • The CockroachDB process runs as the cockroach user (non-root). If the service is absent, disabled, not running, or running as root, this is a finding.

Rule.title: Ensure CockroachDB Cluster is Initialized Securely with TLS
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB clusters must be initialized and operated in secure mode so that all inter- node and client-node communication uses TLS with certificates signed by a trusted CA. CockroachDB's production documentation strongly recommends running secure clusters (with --certs-dir and valid certificates) instead of using --insecure, which disables all encryption and authentication. Nodes must: • Start with valid TLS certificates in a --certs-dir directory: ca.crt, node.crt, node.key. • Use mutual TLS between nodes and TLS between clients and nodes. • Avoid --insecure in all production deployments. The controls in this section establish the baseline secure configuration for CockroachDB using TLS-encrypted TCP/IP communication. Additional hardening options, such as using UNIX domain sockets for local connections, may be introduced in later controls. These options do not replace or invalidate the secure configuration defined here, instead they provide complementary, defense-in- depth enhancements where applicable.
Rationale: Initializing the cluster securely ensures: • TLS is required by default for CockroachDB communication. • A node certificate (TLS 1.3) is required on each node, with hostnames/IPs in CN/SAN and signed by a trusted CA. • Clients and nodes authenticate via certificates or passwords, but node identity is always enforced via TLS certificates in secure mode. The --insecure flag disables all encryption and authentication. This configuration is strictly intended for non-production testing environments and must never be used in a production deployment. Secure initialization ensures: • Encryption in transit for all internode and client-node traffic. • Authenticated membership: only nodes with valid, CA-signed node.crt can join. • Strong access control via cryptographic identities for nodes and (optionally) clients.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Generate the cluster Certificate Authority (CA): The documentation suggests creating two directories on your local machine: certs (for public files) and my-safe-directory (for the private CA key). On a secure workstation: # Create directories for certificates # `certs` : You'll generate your CA certificate and all node and client certificates and keys in this directory. # `my-safe-directory` : You'll generate your CA key in this directory and then reference the key when generating node and client certificates. mkdir certs my-safe-directory # Generate the cluster Certificate Authority (CA) cockroach cert create-ca \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=my-safe-directory/ca.key 2. Generate node certificates for each node (Repeat this block for each node): For each node, issue a multi-purpose node.crt with all relevant addresses and DNS names (node IPs/hostnames, load-balancer addresses, localhost). Example: # NOTE: Replace <node-ip>, <node-hostname>, and <load-balancer> addresses. cockroach cert create-node \ <node-internal-ip> \ <node-external-ip> \ <node-hostname> \ localhost \ 127.0.0.1 \ <load-balancer-ip> \ <load-balancer-hostname> \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=my-safe-directory/ca.key After uploading each node's cert/key, remove or overwrite node.crt/node.key locally before generating the next node's pair, as recommended. 3. Generate client certificate for the root user: cockroach cert create-client \ root \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=my-safe-directory/ca.key This creates client.root.crt and client.root.key, used for secure administrative access. 4. Distribute and Secure Certificates (on each node): On each node, create a certs directory under the Cockroach data directory and upload the appropriate files. The docs commonly use ~/certs or /var/lib/cockroach/certs. ssh <username>@<node-address> "mkdir -p /var/lib/cockroach/certs" scp certs/ca.crt certs/node.crt certs/node.key \ <username>@<node-address>:/var/lib/cockroach/certs Set ownership so the CockroachDB Unix user (e.g., cockroach) owns the directory: chown -R cockroach:cockroach /var/lib/cockroach Optionally copy client.root.* to a secure admin host where you run cockroach sql. Action Command (Run on Local Machine) scp certs/ca.crt certs/node.crt Upload CA and Node Certificates certs/node.key <username>@<node- address>:~/certs rm certs/node.crt certs/node.key (To (Local) Cleanup prepare for the next node's cert generation) scp certs/client.root.crt Upload Client Certificate (for local certs/client.root.key <username>@<node- admin/troubleshooting) address>:~/certs 5. Start and Initialize the Cluster Securely (on each node): 5.1. Start each node with --certs-dir (no --insecure): The service file ( cockroach.service from the previous control) contains the --certs- dir=certs flag and is configured to run from the /var/lib/cockroach working directory: Ensure the ExecStart line includes --certs-dir and excludes --insecure: [Unit] Description=CockroachDB Documentation=https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/ After=network.target [Service] Type=notify User=cockroach Group=cockroach WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/cockroach ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cockroach start \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --advertise-addr=<node-address> \ --join=<node1-address>,<node2-address>,<node3-address> \ --cache=.25 \ --max-sql-memory=.25 TimeoutStopSec=60 Restart=always RestartSec=10 StandardOutput=syslog StandardError=syslog [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target 5.2. Enable and Start the Service Reload the systemd daemon to recognize the configuration, then enable and start the service: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable cockroach.service sudo systemctl start cockroach.service Verify the service is running: systemctl status cockroach.service 5.3. Initialize the cluster securely (Run only once from the local machine) Once all nodes are running, initialize the cluster using the root client certificate. After all nodes are started in secure mode: # Run once from the local machine: cockroach init \ --certs-dir=certs \ --host=<first-node-host> 6. Verify Secure Operation • Use secure client connection (this already proves certs are working): cockroach sql \ --certs-dir=certs \ --host=<node-host> \ -e "SHOW DATABASES;" • Check node status and liveness with --certs-dir: cockroach node status --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs -- host=<node-host> o Cluster ID consistency: cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=<node-host> All nodes should report secure status and the same cluster ID.

check.check-content: 1. Confirm the cluster is not running with --insecure Run the following command on any node: ps -ef | grep cockroach Expected Results: • If --insecure appears, the node is definitely operating insecurely. • If --accept-sql-without-tls appears, o TLS encryption is still used for all traffic. o SQL clients may connect with sslmode=off/cockroach sql --insecure, skipping TLS authentication but not encryption 2. Verify presence and ownership of certificate directory Examples generally use a certs directory under a CockroachDB data directory (e.g., /var/lib/cockroach/certs), owned by the cockroach user. ls -ld /var/lib/cockroach/certs ls -l /var/lib/cockroach/certs Expected Results: • Directory is owned by a dedicated CockroachDB account (e.g., cockroach:cockroach). • Contains at least: ca.crt, node.crt, node.key. For client certs on that host, client.<user>.crt and client.<user>.key (e.g., client.root.*). 3. Validate node certificate against the CA Use OpenSSL to verify that node.crt is signed by the cluster CA: openssl verify -CAfile /var/lib/cockroach/certs/ca.crt /var/lib/cockroach/certs/node.crt Expected Results: /var/lib/cockroach/certs/node.crt: OK • Output shows the node certificate as OK. This aligns with the requirement that node.crt must be signed by ca.crt. 4. Confirm cluster identity and secure connectivity: Use the secure CLI to query node status: cockroach node status --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node-host> If you connect this way to each node (or to different addresses that might represent different clusters), you can compare the Cluster ID line in the welcome message. All nodes that belong to the same cluster must report the same cluster Expected Results: • Command succeeds using certificates (no --insecure). • All nodes you query report the same Cluster ID and nodes are available. The docs note that nodes in the same cluster share a cluster ID; CLI usage with -- certs-dir is the standard secure pattern. cockroach sql \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --host=<node-host> \ -e "SHOW DATABASES;" A successful connection without --insecure confirms secure SQL connectivity.

Rule.title: Do Not Use the --insecure Flag in Production Environments Under Any Circumstances
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB supports an --insecure startup option that disables all node-to-node and client-to-node encryption, authentication, and certificate validation. When started in this mode, the cluster operates entirely without Transport Layer Security (TLS), allowing unauthenticated and unencrypted connections. This option exists only for initial testing or ephemeral local development. It must never be used in production or multi-node environments, where it exposes the cluster to interception, tampering, or unauthorized node participation.
Rationale: Starting CockroachDB with -insecure removes fundamental security controls and nullifies all certificate-based trust relationships. In insecure mode: • Network traffic is transmitted in plaintext. • Nodes can impersonate other nodes and join clusters without verification. • Client authentication is disabled. • Sensitive data (SQL queries, credentials, session tokens) can be read or modified in transit. Running CockroachDB insecurely in production constitutes a critical finding and can result in data compromise, regulatory non-compliance, or full cluster takeover. This reduces the risk of privilege escalation, unauthorized data access, and tampering with sensitive files such as logs, data stores, and TLS certificates.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Stop all insecure nodes: sudo systemctl stop cockroach.service 2. Generate a certificate authority and signed certificates: cockroach cert create-ca \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=my-safe-directory/ca.key cockroach cert create-node \ <addresses/hostnames...> \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=my-safe-directory/ca.key cockroach cert create-client \ root \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=my-safe-directory/ca.key 3. Remove insecure configuration from systemd: Edit the systemd unit file (usually /etc/systemd/system/cockroach.service) to remove --insecure and add --certs-dir. Automated cleanup (use with caution): sudo grep -Rl "--insecure" /etc/systemd/system | xargs sudo sed -i '/-- insecure/d' 4. Manual Configuration (Recommended): Ensure the ExecStart line looks like this: ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cockroach start \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --advertise-addr=<node-address> \ --listen-addr=<node-address>:26357 \ --sql-adr=<node-address>:26257 \ --http-addr=<node-address>:8080 \ --join=<peer-nodes> \ --cache=.25 \ --max-sql-memory=.25 5. Reload and Restart Securely Reload the systemd daemon to apply changes and restart the service: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl start cockroach.service 6. Initialize the cluster securely (if new) If this is a fresh cluster being converted to secure mode before initialization: cockroach init \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --host=<first-node-host> 7. Remove any insecure startup configuration: sudo grep -Rl "--insecure" /etc/systemd/system | xargs sudo sed -i '/-- insecure/d' sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart cockroach.service 8. Verify secure operation: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/car/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> -e \ "select node_id, field as property, substr(value,1,36) as value \ from crdb_internal.node_build_info \ where field='ClusterID' \ order by 1,2;" Expected Results: All nodes should share the same Cluster ID and report secure status.

check.check-content: 1. Check for --insecure usage: ps -ef | grep cockroach | grep -- '--insecure' Findings if: No output. If --insecure appears in any process command line, this is a finding. 2. Review logs for insecure startup warnings: grep -i "insecure mode" /var/lib/cockroach/logs/cockroach.log Expected Results: No entries indicating "* WARNING: RUNNING IN INSECURE MODE!".

Rule.title: Ensure All Cluster Nodes Are Running the Exact Same Version, Including the Patch Release Number
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>All CockroachDB nodes in a self-hosted cluster must run the same major, minor, and patch version of the CockroachDB binary. The docs explicitly recommend that "all cluster nodes are running exactly the same CockroachDB version, including the patch release version number," and call out version mismatch as an essential alert condition. Mixed versions usually occur when: • A rolling upgrade was started but not completed. • Some nodes were missed during upgrade or restarted with an outdated binary. • Manual differences in binaries were introduced. CockroachDB supports rolling upgrades by updating one node at a time, but the expectation is that after the upgrade is complete, all nodes are on the same patch version.
Rationale: Maintaining version consistency across all cluster nodes ensures that: • Consensus protocols (Raft) and replication mechanisms function correctly. • All nodes interpret metadata, schema changes, and internal APIs consistently. • Security patches and bug fixes are uniformly applied across the cluster. • Operational procedures such as backups, restores, and upgrades behave predictably. Running nodes on mixed patch versions introduces operational risks such as: • Split-brain conditions or inconsistent data state across replicas. • Feature mismatches (newer nodes using RPCs unsupported by older peers). • Failed schema migrations or upgrade finalization errors. Version uniformity is a key production readiness requirement defined by Cockroach Labs for cluster stability and compliance with enterprise-grade support contracts</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Identify out-of-date nodes: cockroach node status --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> -- format=table Review build or version fields to locate mismatched nodes. 2. Download the latest consistent binary Please refer to Control 1.1 3. Perform a rolling restart (Upgrade one node at a time.): • Use cockroach node drain with --shutdown to gracefully drain and then terminate the node's process. • Replace the binary, then restart via your process manager (systemd, etc.). 3.1. Drain the node and terminate the process: cockroach node drain <node-id> \ --shutdown \ --host= {address of any live node} \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs This uses cockroach node drain to: • Drain the node. • Then shut down the cockroach process automatically because of --shutdown. 3.2. Replace the binary On that node: Install or copy the new cockroach binary in place of the old one (e.g., /var/lib/cockroach) 3.3. Restart the node via your process manager For a systemd-managed service: systemctl start cockroach.service (Use your actual service name, e.g., cockroach as configured in your unit file.) 3.4. Verify the node has rejoined and is ready After a short wait, confirm the node is serving SQL: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<upgraded-node> \ -e "SELECT 1;" Repeat for the next node until all nodes have been drained, shut down, upgraded, and restarted with the new binary. 4. Verify all nodes now run the same version: After completing the rolling procedure: Use the DB Console Node List to confirm that every node now reports the same CockroachDB version and build. If your monitoring is configured per the Version mismatch alert guidance, it should no longer fire once all build timestamps are aligned. 5. Finalize the cluster upgrade (if applicable): If this remediation is part of a major-version upgrade and you have disabled auto-finalization (for example, via cluster.auto_upgrade.enabled = false), then once all nodes are on the new binary and healthy, you must finalize: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> -e "SET CLUSTER SETTING version = '{VERSION}';" Replace {VERSION} with the new major version, such as 25.4 Finalization completes when: • SHOW CLUSTER SETTING version returns the new version, and • All migration and schema change jobs have reached terminal states.

check.check-content: 1. Check the CockroachDB version running on each node: From any node host you can run: cockroach version Or The DB Console ( Cluster Overview → Node List) shows each node's version. You should verify that all nodes are on the same version before starting an upgrade and to use the DB Console Node List to confirm uniformity. Expected Results: All nodes should report the same CockroachDB version before and during an upgrade. If any node is on a different version, that indicates an incomplete or inconsistent upgrade and must be corrected before proceeding. 3. Check upgrade status: • For major-version upgrades: o The upgrade is not complete until finalized (or auto-finalization completes). o Finalization is done by setting the version cluster setting to the new major version, or by allowing auto-finalization to run. To check the cluster's logical version: cockroach sql --certs-dir=//var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> -e \ "SHOW CLUSTER SETTING version;" Expected Results: • After a completed major upgrade, this shows the new major version (e.g., 24.3 or 25.4 depending on docs/release) • If it still shows the prior major version, finalization has not completed, and some migration jobs may still be running.

Rule.title: Establish a Process for Rolling Upgrades to Apply Security Patches Without Downtime
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB supports rolling upgrades, allowing administrators to apply security patches, minor version updates, and configuration changes without cluster downtime. A rolling upgrade updates one node at a time, while the remaining nodes continue serving traffic and maintaining quorum. Establishing a formal, documented rolling upgrade process ensures consistent patch application, reduces service disruption, and maintains the cluster's integrity and availability. This process must include pre-upgrade validation, stepwise node restarts, health verification, and post-upgrade finalization.
Rationale: A defined rolling upgrade process: • Ensures security patches and bug fixes are applied consistently across nodes. • Maintains continuous availability by preserving quorum during upgrades. • Prevents version drift and configuration inconsistencies. • Enables safe rollback or recovery in case of unexpected upgrade failures. • Reduces operational risk while maintaining compliance with patch management policies. Without a controlled rolling upgrade process: • Clusters may suffer unplanned downtime, split-brain events, or data unavailability. • Nodes could run outdated, unpatched binaries, exposing vulnerabilities. • Partial upgrades could lead to inconsistent Raft or schema states.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Prepare for rolling upgrade: • Confirm cluster health and full replication: cockroach node status --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> cockroach node status --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --all Backups are strongly recommended before upgrades. 2. Upgrade CockroachDB binary on each node (one at a time): • Use cockroach node drain with --shutdown to gracefully drain and then terminate the node's process. • Replace the binary, then restart via your process manager (systemd, etc.). 2.1. Drain the node and terminate the process: cockroach node drain <node-id> \ --shutdown \ --host= {address of any live node} \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs This uses cockroach node drain to: • Drain the node. • Then shut down the cockroach process automatically because of --shutdown. 2.2. Replace the binary On that node (Follow Control 1.1): Install or copy the new cockroach binary in place of the old one (e.g., /var/lib/cockroach) 2.3. Restart the node via your process manager For a systemd-managed service: systemctl start cockroach.service (Use your actual service name, e.g., cockroach as configured in your unit file.) 2.4. Verify the node has rejoined and is ready After a short wait, confirm the node is serving SQL: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<upgraded-node> \ -e "SELECT 1;" Iterate through the remaining nodes, ensuring that each node is drained, shut down, upgraded, and restarted. To ensure data availability, strictly enforce a wait period after each restart until the cluster reports no under-replicated ranges before attempting to upgrade the subsequent node. Expected Results: Node shows is_available : true and matches the new build tag. 3. Finalize the cluster version after all nodes upgraded: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> SET CLUSTER SETTING version = '{VERSION}';" Replace {VERSION} with the new major version, such as 25.4 4. Verify upgrade success: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> \ -e "SHOW CLUSTER SETTING version;"

check.check-content: Run the following checks: 1. Verify presence of a documented upgrade procedure Confirm your organization has a written or automated process for performing rolling upgrades, including: • Stepwise node restarts (one node at a time). • Verification commands and pre/post checks. • Defined rollback plan. • Reference to Cockroach Labs' upgrade documentation. Review operational runbooks or CI/CD pipelines. 2. Check CockroachDB cluster health before upgrade: cockroach node status --certs-dir="certs" --all Expected Results: All nodes report the same version, is_available: true, and the cluster is fully replicated. 3. Verify rolling upgrade sequence logs exist: grep -i "upgrade" /var/lib/cockroach/logs/cockroach.log Expected Results: Log entries should show sequential node restarts, not simultaneous restarts across all nodes. 4. Confirm upgrade finalization post-process: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> -e "SHOW CLUSTER SETTING version;" Expected Results: Cluster version matches the upgraded binary version.

Rule.title: Ensure Encryption at Rest Keys Are Managed by an External KMS and Retrieved at Startup
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB supports the use of external key management systems (KMS), such as HashiCorp Vault, to securely manage and deliver encryption keys used for encryption at rest. External key managers provide a centralized and auditable way to store and rotate keys and supply them dynamically to CockroachDB at startup. By retrieving keys securely at runtime instead of storing them on local disks or in configuration files, administrators can reduce the risk of key exposure and strengthen compliance with data protection standards.
Rationale: Managing encryption keys within the same host that stores the encrypted data increases risk in the event of a host or filesystem compromise. Integrating CockroachDB with an external KMS ensures that: • Encryption keys are not stored in plaintext on local systems. • Keys can be rotated and revoked centrally. • Only authorized CockroachDB nodes can access the keys at runtime. • Audit trails record every key access for accountability and compliance. Without a secure external key manager, any compromise of a database node could reveal local key material and allow attackers to decrypt sensitive data.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Deploy or connect to a supported key management system: Such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS, or another trusted external provider. 2. Configure the Systemd Service to enable encryption: Edit the service file at /etc/systemd/system/cockroach.service. Update the ExecStart command to include the --enterprise-encryption flag: Example Configuration (File-based key on separate volume): ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cockroach start \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --store=/var/lib/cockroach \ --enterprise-encryption=path=/var/lib/cockroach,key=/secure-keys/crdb- store.key,old-key=plain \ --advertise-addr=<node-address> \ --listen-addr=<node-address>:26357 \ --http-addr=<node-address>:8080 \ --sql-adr=<node-address>:26257 \ --join=<peer-nodes> old-key=plain is used only when first enabling encryption on an existing plaintext cluster to allow rotation. Once encrypted, remove old-key=plain. 3. Secure the key files If using local key files (instead of a direct KMS integration), ensure they are strictly protected: # Create a secure directory separate from data sudo mkdir -p /secure-keys # Move/Generate key sudo mv /path/to/generated.key /secure-keys/crdb-store.key # Restrict permissions sudo chown -R cockroach:cockroach /secure-keys sudo chmod 700 /secure-keys sudo chmod 400 /secure-keys/crdb-store.key 4. Reload and Restart Reload systemd and restart the service to apply encryption: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart cockroach.service 5. Verify encryption status: Use the CockroachDB debug tooling to validate that encryption is active and that a store key is in use. cockroach debug encryption-active-key /var/lib/cockroach Expected Results: Encryption is active and keys are sourced from the external KMS.

check.check-content: 1. Check for enterprise encryption configuration: ps -ef | grep cockroach | grep -- '--enterprise-encryption' Expected Results: Each CockroachDB process for encrypted stores includes a --enterprise- encryption=path =...,key =...,old-key =...,rotation-period=... argument. Note: Note: Once --enterprise-encryption has been configured for a store, it must always be present on that node. 2. Inspect configuration for external key source: # Look for Vault, Transit, or other secret loader references grep -Ri "vault" /etc/cockroach /usr/lib/systemd/system grep -Ri "encryption-key" /etc/cockroach /usr/lib/systemd/system Expected Results: You may find references to Vault (or another secret delivery mechanism) in: • systemd unit files (e.g., ExecStartPre scripts fetching keys), • wrapper scripts under /etc/cockroach, • environment variables that point to Vault or a secret loader. 3. Verify that local key files are not present: # Look for key files under Cockroach-related paths find /etc/cockroach /var/lib/cockroach -type f -name "*.key" -ls Expected Results: • Store key files do exist somewhere (since self-hosted Enterprise Encryption at Rest requires them). • They are: o Not on the same partition/drive as the data directory (e.g., /var/lib/cockroach). o Protected by file permissions: owned by the CockroachDB user, not world- readable. • If you find key files inside the data directory or on the same volume, that is a finding to remediate.

Rule.title: Ensure Network Time Protocol (NTP) Service Is Configured for Cluster Clock Synchronization
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB requires moderate levels of clock synchronization to preserve data consistency. When a node detects that its clock is out of sync with at least half of the other nodes in the cluster by 80% of the maximum offset allowed (500 ms by default), it will spontaneously shut down to avoid consistency anomalies. Administrators must run clock synchronization software (for example, NTP or chrony) on each node and use compatible time sources (e.g. Google Public NTP, Amazon Time Sync Service) that implement leap-second smearing consistently across the cluster. CockroachDB does not install or configure NTP automatically, this must be done at the OS or platform level.
Rationale: Accurate clock synchronization is critical for CockroachDB to ensure: • Serializable transactions: Prevents transaction overlap errors. • Reliable Raft consensus: Ensures proper election and replication timing. • Accurate event logs: Enables consistent auditing and troubleshooting. • Automatic fault detection: Prevents unnecessary node shutdowns caused by clock drift. Without NTP, clock skew can cause transaction uncertainty, stale reads, data inconsistencies, or even cluster instability.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: Key requirements: • Run one clock sync service (NTP/chrony or provider's built-in time source) on each node. • Use compatible, leap-smearing time sources across all nodes. 1. Install and enable a time sync service (per environment): • AWS EC2: Configure each instance to use Amazon Time Sync Service via 169.254.169.123, verify via c hronyc sources -v. • GCE: use GCE's internal NTP via metadata.google.internal; optionally Google Public NTP ( time.google.com) for non-GCE nodes. • On-prem / DigitalOcean / Azure: install NTP (or chrony) and configure Google Public NTP ( time[1-4].google.com) as the source. 2. Configure trusted, compatible NTP sources: Follow the environment-specific doc: • Use: o Amazon Time Sync on AWS. o GCP internal NTP on GCE. o Google Public NTP ( time.google.com, time1-4.google.com) elsewhere. • Ensure all nodes are synced either: o To the same time source, or o To sources that implement leap second smearing in the same way (Google and Amazon are compatible with each other but not with default NTP pool). 3. Restart and verify the time service: Use your OS commands (for example, systemctl restart chronyd then chronyc sources -v, or timedatectl) to verify: • The service is running on all nodes. • Nodes are synchronized to the intended sources (e.g., 169.254.169.123 for AWS, time*.google.com for Google NTP). 4. Validate CockroachDB cluster offset: Clock offsets, as observed via Prometheus metrics or the DB Console, are well below the configured --max-offset (500 ms by default). 5. (Optional hardening): • Prefer internal/enterprise NTP sources or cloud-provider services (Amazon Time Sync, Google internal NTP). • If not using Google/AWS services, configure chrony with client-side leap smearing, identically on all nodes. 5. (Optional) Harden configuration using authenticated or internal NTP sources for production deployments.

check.check-content: Key Requirement: • Some clock sync service (NTP, chrony, etc.) is running on each node. • All nodes are synchronized to compatible, leap-smearing time sources (e.g., Amazon Time Sync, Google internal/public NTP), or chrony with client-side smearing configured consistently. • Clock offsets stay within the configured --max-offset. 1. Confirm an NTP/chrony service is active (platform/OS-specific): Use your OS tools (for example, systemctl status chronyd, timedatectl, etc.) to ensure one clock sync service is enabled and running on each node. 2. Verify time source selection and leap-second behavior: Check that all nodes use: • Amazon Time Sync Service on AWS. • Google internal NTP on GCE, or Google Public NTP elsewhere. • Or chrony with client-side leap smearing if your time source does not smear server-side, configured the same way on all nodes 3. Inspect CockroachDB's view of clock offsets The --max-offset flag is a startup parameter for the cockroach start command, with a default value of 500 milliseconds (ms). To inspect clock offsets between nodes, use Prometheus metrics such as clock_offset_meannanos or view the Clock Offset graph in the DB Console. These tools provide visibility into clock synchronization and help ensure offsets remain well below the configured --max-offset Expected Results: Offsets are well below the configured --max-offset (500 ms by default). 4. Check logs for clock skew errors: grep -i "clock" /var/lib/cockroach/logs/cockroach.log Expected Results: No entries indicating that a node is "more than 400ms away from at least half of the known nodes" or similar clock-offset errors.

Rule.title: Ensure Each CockroachDB Node Runs as a Dedicated Process on a Separate Host
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>For all self-hosted VM or bare-metal production deployments (on-premises or on cloud providers like AWS, GCP, Azure), each CockroachDB node must run as a single, dedicated cockroach start process on its own physical or virtual machine (VM). It is a critical violation of best practices to co-locate multiple CockroachDB node processes on the same host, as this undermines the database's high-availability design and fault tolerance. Additionally, the data directory/storage volume for each node must be unique and not shared across any other node.
Rationale: CockroachDB's distributed consensus mechanism (Raft) and replication model are fundamentally built on the assumption that each node is an independent failure domain. • Single Point of Failure (SPOF): Running multiple nodes on the same VM turns that single host into an SPOF. A simple hardware failure, OS crash, or kernel panic on that host could simultaneously take down multiple data replicas, potentially eliminating the quorum required for the cluster to remain available. • Undermined Fault Tolerance: Co-location means data ranges (replicas) are not properly isolated. This defeats the purpose of maintaining multiple replicas across different failure zones. • Resource Contention: Sharing CPU, I/O, and network resources among multiple node processes can lead to unpredictable latency, performance issues, and conflicts. • Data Corruption Risk: Sharing the same data directory (--store path) between two or more active node processes will lead to locking errors and data corruption.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: If any host is found to be running more than one cockroach start process, or if storage is shared: 1. Stop Extra CockroachDB Processes: On the overloaded host, identify and stop the excess node processes: # Identify all cockroach start processes ps -ef | grep '[c]ockroach start' # Stop via systemd if used (assuming only one service should remain) systemctl stop cockroach.service 2. Provision Separate VMs and Re-deploy: The nodes that were stopped must be moved to their own dedicated infrastructure: • Provision a new VM or host for each node that was sharing a machine. • Install CockroachDB on the new host. • Configure your virtualization platform (e.g., VMware, Hyper-V) to enforce Anti- Affinity rules. This guarantees that no two CockroachDB VMs are ever scheduled to run on the same underlying physical host. This prevents a single hardware failure from taking down multiple nodes. • Create a dedicated, unique data directory and ensure proper ownership before starting the node: mkdir /var/lib/cockroach useradd cockroach chown -R cockroach /var/lib/cockroach 3. Start Each Node as a Single Service on Its Own Host: Use a single cockroach start per machine, either manually or via systemd. For example (secure on-premises): cockroach start \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --store=/var/lib/cockroach \ --advertise-addr=<node-ip-address>:26257 \ --listen-addr=10.0.0.1:26357 \ # Note: This configuration is discussed in a further control --sql-addr=192.168.1.1:26257 \ # Note: This configuration is discussed in a further control --join=<node1-addr>,<node2-addr>,<node3-addr> \ --cache=.25 \ --max-sql-memory=.25 \ --background Or using the systemd service template from the docs, with one instance per host and -- advertise-addr set to that host's address. (Control 1.2) 4. Ensure Storage is Not Shared Verify that the --store directory on the new host points to a local, dedicated disk or partition that is not mounted or accessible by any other CockroachDB node. • For each node, allocate its own disk or partition. • Start the node with one or more --store flags referencing that host's local storage. Separate --store per disk and warn that you cannot later " scale down " stores without decommissioning the node. Do not mount the same data directory for multiple nodes, even across different hosts.

check.check-content: Perform the following checks on every host intended to run a CockroachDB node: 1. Verify that only one CockroachDB process is active per host: #Check for active "cockroach start" processes on the VM: ps -ef | grep '[c]ockroach start' Expected Results: At most one cockroach start process per VM. 2. Verify Data Directories Are Isolated: #Examine the data directory paths used by the node process (e.g., the default "/var/lib/cockroach" or a custom "--store" path): ls -ld /var/lib/cockroach # Also check any other custom store paths Expected Results: • Each CockroachDB node process may use one or more unique data directories by specifying multiple --store flags (for example, when using multiple disks or SSDs on a single node). • Each data directory or disk must be dedicated to a single node process and must not be shared with any other CockroachDB node process or host. Sharing a data directory or disk between node processes is not supported and can lead to data corruption or operational issues 3. Confirm Topology Design: From your deployment design and inventory, verify that the number of VMs equals the number of CockroachDB nodes. All self-hosted deployment guides state that each node should run on a separate VM or machine Expected Results: • The number of dedicated VMs (or physical hosts) must equal the number of CockroachDB nodes deployed. • There should be no documented or intentional design to run multiple node processes on a single VM.

Rule.title: Do Not Grant Sudo Privileges to the CockroachDB Process User
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB should run under a dedicated, non-root operating system account that has only the permissions required to read and write CockroachDB's data, log, and certificate directories. This dedicated service user (commonly cockroach) must not be granted sudo privileges or be included in any privileged system groups (such as wheel, sudo, or adm). Allowing the CockroachDB service account to escalate privileges could enable an attacker who compromises the database process to gain full control of the underlying host. This violates the principle of least privilege and undermines system isolation.
Rationale: Restricting the CockroachDB service account to minimal privileges ensures that even if the CockroachDB process or a client connection is compromised, the attacker cannot: • Escalate to root access. • Modify system configurations or kernel parameters. • Access sensitive files outside CockroachDB directories. • Install or execute arbitrary system commands. This control upholds operating system-level separation between application processes and administrative privileges, reducing the risk of full system compromise.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Create a dedicated non-privileged account for CockroachDB if it does not already exist: # Create Cockroach directory mkdir -p /var/lib/cockroach # Create a Unix user named 'cockroach' useradd cockroach # Make the directory owned by 'cockroach' chown -R cockroach /var/lib/cockroach The docs use useradd cockroach directly; you may additionally configure shell/flags to fit your distro standards. 2. Remove any sudo privileges for the CockroachDB user: Edit /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d/* and delete any entries granting CockroachDB ALL privileges. For example, remove lines such as: • Edit /etc/sudoers or ``/etc/security/limits.d/cockroach.conf`: cockroach ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL • Log out and back in, or restart the CockroachDB process to apply. 3. Verify service operation: Ensure the CockroachDB systemd unit runs as the cockroach user and group: grep -E 'User=|Group=' /etc/systemd/system/cockroach.service Ensure the output: User=cockroach Group=cockroach Expected Results: User=cockroach Group=cockroach Reload systemd and restart CockroachDB if changes are made: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart cockroach

check.check-content: Perform the following checks on each CockroachDB node to verify that the process user does not have sudo or root-level privileges: # 1. Identify the CockroachDB process user ps -eo user,comm | grep '[c]ockroach' # 2. Verify the user's UID is non-root (should not be 0) id -u cockroach # Expected: A non-zero value (e.g., 997) # Inspect the systemd unit to confirm non-root user sudo systemctl cat cockroach | grep -E '^User=|^Group=' #Expected : User=cockroach ; Group=cockroach # 3. Check if the user belongs to privileged groups id cockroach # Ensure groups like 'sudo', 'wheel', or 'adm' are NOT listed. # 4. Verify that the user does not have sudo permissions sudo -l -U cockroach Expected Results: • The CockroachDB process runs under a dedicated non-root user (e.g., cockroach). • The user is not a member of any privileged system groups. • The sudo -l command returns "user cockroach is not allowed to run sudo" or a similar denial message. If the CockroachDB service account can execute commands as root or escalate privileges, this is a finding.

Rule.title: Ensure Database Servers Are Isolated in a Separate Subnet with Restricted Ingress and Egress
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The core requirement is to deploy CockroachDB nodes on private, non-public networks (subnets, VLANs, or VPC private segments) and to use strict firewall or security group rules to control access to the required ports. This ensures the database is shielded from the public internet and enforces least-privilege access. For enhanced security, it is a best practice to separate the listen address for inter- node communication from the listen address used for client SQL connections. The three critical TCP ports to control are: • 26257 (SQL Traffic): Must be accessible only to application servers, and authorized load balancers. • 8080 (DB Console): Must be highly restricted, ideally accessible only by administrator networks or via secure tunneling (e.g., SSH). • Other Port (e.g. 26357): Must be accessible only by other CockroachDB nodes.
Rationale: Network segmentation limits the blast radius of a compromise and prevents direct exposure of database nodes to the public Internet or untrusted systems. By isolating CockroachDB in a dedicated subnet, you: • Reduce the attack surface available to external threats. • Prevent lateral movement from compromised web/app servers. • Enforce least-privilege access paths between tiers. • Support compliance requirements for network zoning and data-plane isolation. Improperly exposing CockroachDB to shared or public networks can result in unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or denial-of-service attacks.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Place CockroachDB Nodes in Private Networks: Ensure all CockroachDB VMs are located in a private VLAN or non-internet-routable subnet. If a public IP is assigned for management, ensure it is not the primary address used for cluster communication and that its inbound ports are fully locked down. 2. Tighten Inbound Access: Configure host-based firewalls or network security groups to enforce the principle of least-privilege: • For Port 26257/TCP: o Permit: Inbound traffic only from the IP ranges/security groups associated with: ▪ The other CockroachDB nodes. ▪ Load balancers (if applicable). o Deny: All other traffic by default. • For Port 8080/TCP (DB Console): o Permit: Inbound traffic only from specific, known admin IP ranges (e.g., VPN gateways or jump hosts). o Highly Recommended: Block direct external access and require administrators to use an SSH tunnel to securely access the DB Console via a jump host. • For Other Port (26357/TCP): o Permit: Inbound traffic only from the IP ranges/security groups associated with: ▪ The other CockroachDB nodes. 3. Separate Internal and SQL Ports CockroachDB allows you to separate the listen address for internal inter-node communication from the listen address used for client connections connections. This is the best practice for granular security control. • --listen-addr: Defines the address and port used for inter-node (cluster) communication. Restrict this port to only allow traffic from other CockroachDB nodes. • --sql-addr: Defines the address and port used for client SQL connections. Restrict this port to only allow traffic from application servers or load balancers. Example Command: cockroach start \ --listen-addr=10.0.0.1:26357 \ --sql-addr=192.168.1.1:26257 \ This configuration allows you to: • Block all external access to 10.0.0.1:26357 (the inter-node port), only allowing traffic from the internal IP range of other nodes. • Restrict access to 192.168.1.1:26257 (the SQL port) to application servers and load balancers. 4. Restrict Outbound Access: Following general security hardening principles, implement a restrictive egress policy: • Allow: Outbound traffic only to necessary services (e.g., NTP, S3/GCS/Azure Blob for backups, monitoring/logging endpoints). • Deny: All other outbound traffic by default.

check.check-content: Perform the following checks to confirm CockroachDB nodes are deployed in a dedicated subnet or network segment with restrictive security rules. 1. Identify CockroachDB Node Addresses and Network Placement: • Check Node IPs: Use the cockroach node status command to list the addresses the cluster is using for communication. cockroach node status \ --certs-dir=/path/to/certs \ --host=<node-address> \ --format=table Expected Results: Confirm the node addresses are internal/private (e.g., RFC 1918 ranges like 10.x.x.x, 172.16.x.x, or 192.168.x.x) and are consistent with your controlled internal network segments (VLANs or VPC private subnets). 2. Review Ingress Firewall / Security Group Rules: Review the host-level firewalls (e.g., iptables, firewalld) or cloud security groups (AWS, GCP, Azure) applied to the CockroachDB nodes. Required Ingress Sources Port Purpose Finding if (Must be restricted) Only permit ingress from SQL Open to 0.0.0.0/0 or 26257/TCP Application Servers and Load Clients untrusted public networks. Balancers. Open to 0.0.0.0/0 or DB Admin IP ranges only or local 8080/TCP accessible from non- Console host (if using an SSH tunnel). admin networks. Other Port (e.g. Inter- Other CockroachDB Nodes Open to 0.0.0.0/0 or 26357/TCP) node (for cluster sync). untrusted public networks. 3. Review Egress Rules: Review network perimeter devices (or security groups) controlling outbound traffic from the CockroachDB subnet. Expected Results: Egress is generally restricted, allowing traffic only to required external services (e.g., NTP servers, object storage for backups, monitoring endpoints).

Rule.title: Disable Linux Memory Swapping to Prevent Performance and Stability Issues
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>For production CockroachDB deployments on Linux VMs or bare-metal, it is a critical requirement to disable Linux memory swapping or ensure the system has adequate RAM to prevent swap usage. Swapping database memory pages to slow disk I/O introduces severe and unpredictable latency, compromising the database's performance and stability. The core strategy is to: • Provision sufficient physical RAM ( minimum 4 GiB RAM per vCPU in production). • Configure CockroachDB's memory limits ( --cache and --max-sql-memory) conservatively to prevent the process from exceeding available RAM.
Rationale: Memory swapping introduces unpredictable I/O latency when data is paged to disk. In CockroachDB, this can lead to: • Increased transaction latency or timeouts. • Node unresponsiveness or crash loops under memory contention. • Delayed Raft consensus and loss of quorum availability. Disabling swap guarantees that memory access is always from physical RAM, ensuring consistent performance and preventing severe performance regressions during heavy load. This aligns with Cockroach Labs' production guidance and CIS system hardening principles for high-performance database systems.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Ensure Adequate RAM and Tune Limits: • Provisioning: Upgrade hardware or VM resources to meet the 4 GiB RAM per vCPU requirement. • Tuning: Adjust the --cache and --max-sql-memory flags in the cockroach start command to adhere to the 80% safety margin. Example: On a 16 GiB RAM VM, the limit is 16 GiB * 0.8 = 12.8 GiB. • Set --cache=0.25 ( 4 GiB) • Set --max-sql-memory=0.25 ( 4 GiB) • Total check: (2* 4 GiB) + 4 GiB = 12 GiB. This is safely below 12.8 GiB. 2. Disable Swap Permanently: Apply the standard Linux hardening procedure to disable swap on the host: • Temporarily Disable Swap: Use the swapoff command to immediately disable all active swap devices: sudo swapoff -a • Permanently Disable Swap: Edit the /etc/fstab file and comment out or remove the line corresponding to the swap partition or swap file. This prevents the OS from activating swap on reboot. # Open /etc/fstab in a text editor (e.g., nano or vi) sudo nano /etc/fstab # Locate and comment out the swap entry (add a '#' at the start) # /dev/mapper/centos-swap swap swap defaults 0 0 <-- This line should be commented • Reboot the host to confirm the changes are persistent, then re-run the audit step ( sudo swapon --show).

check.check-content: 1. Perform the following commands on each CockroachDB node to verify that swap is disabled: # 1. Check current swap status sudo swapon --show # 2. Confirm kernel swap configuration cat /proc/swaps Expected Results: swapon --show and /proc/swaps produce no output, indicating no active swap devices. 2. Verify Physical RAM Sizing vs. vCPU: Compare the node's RAM to Cockroach Labs' minimum production recommendation: • At least 4 GiB RAM per vCPU for production nodes. • 2 GiB per vCPU is only acceptable for testing, not production. 3. Check CockroachDB Memory Configuration Inspect the node's startup configuration (e.g., the systemd service file) for the memory allocation flags. Formula Check: The total estimated maximum memory usage for the CockroachDB process should not exceed 80% of system RAM. (2 × --max-sql-memory) + --cache <= 80% of system RAM • --cache (Pebble block cache): Should be set to 25% or higher of system RAM. • --max-sql-memory (SQL temporary data): Should be set to ensure the total formula is met. If the calculated memory usage exceeds 80% of RAM, or if --cache is below 25% of RAM, it is a finding.

Rule.title: Configure Transparent Huge Pages (THP) to madvise to Avoid Increased Memory Usage
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Linux Transparent Huge Pages (THP) is a kernel feature that automatically manages large memory pages to improve performance for some workloads. However, for databases such as CockroachDB, this behavior can cause unpredictable latency spikes, increased memory fragmentation, and excessive CPU overhead due to THP defragmentation. Cockroach Labs recommends configuring THP to madvise instead of the default always mode. This allows CockroachDB to control when huge pages are used without forcing the kernel to automatically allocate them for all processes.
Rationale: THP in always mode may result in: • Unwanted latency from page compaction and defragmentation. • Increased memory consumption under load. • CPU overhead when the kernel continually attempts to merge pages. Setting THP to madvise ensures CockroachDB explicitly requests huge pages when beneficial while maintaining predictable memory performance and reducing kernel overhead. This configuration aligns with production best practices for database workloads and CIS Linux performance hardening standards.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Temporarily set THP to madvise (takes effect immediately): On each node (run as root or via sudo): echo madvise | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled #Optionally, align the defrag behavior: echo madvise | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag 2. Persist the setting across reboots Use your distribution's standard method (for example, systemd unit, boot-time script, or vendor-recommended approach) to ensure enabled is set to madvise at boot. Cockroach Labs notes that the method for permanently changing the THP setting depends on the OS, please refer to the OS documentations. 3. Verify the configuration after reboot: cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled Confirm that madvise remains the active selection.

check.check-content: Perform the following commands on each CockroachDB node to verify THP configuration: # 1. Check the current THP mode cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled # 2. Check the defrag setting cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag Expected Results: The enabled line should show madvise as the active mode, for example: Example output: always madvise [never] Or madvise [never] The exact formatting may vary by kernel, but madvise should be the selected (bracketed) option. If [ always ] is selected (for example, [always] madvise never), this deviates from the CockroachDB recommendation and is a finding for new deployments or for existing deployments without a comfortable memory margin.

Rule.title: Set the File Descriptor Limit to at Least 15,000 to Accommodate Cluster Growth
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB can use a large number of open file descriptors, often more than is available by default. Therefore, note the following recommendations. For each CockroachDB node: • At a minimum, the file descriptors limit must be 1956 (1700 per store plus 256 for networking). If the limit is below this threshold, the node will not start. • It is recommended to set the file descriptors limit to unlimited; otherwise, the recommended limit is at least 15000 (10000 per store plus 5000 for networking). This higher limit ensures performance and accommodates cluster growth. • When the file descriptors limit is not high enough to allocate the recommended amounts, CockroachDB allocates 10000 per store and the rest for networking; if this would result in networking getting less than 256, CockroachDB instead allocates 256 for networking and evenly splits the rest across stores.
Rationale: Failing to configure adequate FD limits can lead to critical operational issues: • Startup Failures: If the hard limit is below the minimum of 1956, the CockroachDB node will explicitly refuse to start. • Operational Instability: Low limits prevent the cluster from accommodating growth in storage (more stores) and network connections, leading to runtime failures under load. • Performance Assurance: The recommended limit of $\ge 15,000$ ensures performance and stability as the cluster scales.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Set per-process limit: To adjust the file descriptors limit for a single process on Linux, enable PAM user limits and set the hard limit to the recommendation mentioned above. Note that CockroachDB always uses the hard limit, so it's not technically necessary to adjust the soft limit, although we do so in the steps below. For example, for a node with 1 stores, we would set the hard limit to at least 15000 (10000 per store and 5000 for networking) as follows: The docs distinguish between systemd-managed and non-systemd setups. • If you use systemd: Manually-set limits set using the ulimit command or a configuration file like /etc/limits.conf are ignored for services started by systemd. To limit the number of open file descriptors, add a line like the following to the service definition for the cockroach process: LimitNOFILE=15000 You may also set LimitNOFILE=INFINITY if you have tested that configuration with a realistic workload. Reload systemd for the new limit to take effect: sudo systemctl daemon-reload Restart the CockroachDB service: sudo systemctl restart cockroach.service • If you do not use systemd: Edit /etc/security/limits.conf and append the following lines to the file: * soft nofile 15000 * hard nofile 15000 You can replace * with the specific username that runs CockroachDB (for example, cockroach). Then: Ensure pam_limits.so is enabled in /etc/pam.d/common-session and common- session-noninteractive: session required pam_limits.so Reboot or log out / log back in and restart the CockroachDB process, then verify with ulimit -a. 2. Increase system-wide file descriptor limit: You should also confirm that the file descriptors limit for the entire Linux system is at least 10 times higher than the per-process limit documented above (e.g., at least 150000). • If using systemd, add in /etc/systemd/system.conf or a drop-in for the Manager service: [Manager] LimitNOFILE=150000 Then: sudo systemctl daemon-reload • If not using systemd: cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max # check current echo 150000 | sudo tee /proc/sys/fs/file-max To persist, configure your distribution's sysctl settings accordingly. 3. Verify: After changes: cat /proc/$(pgrep cockroach)/limits | grep "open files" cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max Confirm: • Process hard limit for open files ≥ 15000. • System-wide file- max ≥ 10× that value.

check.check-content: Perform the following checks on each CockroachDB node: 1. Check CockroachDB's Active Per-Process Hard Limit: Use the standard Linux process limits interface: cat /proc/$(pgrep cockroach)/limits | grep "open files" Expected Results: The 'Max open files' Hard limit must be ≥ 15000(or the value you have set, if higher). 2. Check systemd service LimitNOFILE (if using systemd): Inspect your unit file (for example, /var/systemd/system/cockroach.service or similar): sudo systemctl cat cockroach | grep -i LimitNOFILE 3. Verify System-Wide FD Limit: The system-wide file descriptor limit should be at least 10× the per- process limit (e.g., ≥ 150000 when using 15000 per process) cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max Expected Results: If the CockroachDB process hard limit is < 15000, or the system-wide limit is too low to support that many FDs per process, this is a finding.

Rule.title: Ensure CockroachDB Logging Is Enabled and Logs Are Securely Stored
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB's built-in logging must remain enabled to capture database events, and log files should be stored in a secure location with appropriate access restrictions. By default, CockroachDB produces log files for subsystems such as SQL, authentication, and cluster events. Although logging cannot be fully disabled, misconfiguration (e.g., setting --log-dir= empty or invalid) can prevent logs from being retained. Ensuring that logging is active and directed to a secure directory provides an audit trail of activity. Only the CockroachDB service account and authorized administrators should have access.
Rationale: Logs record authentication attempts, configuration changes, and operational events. Disabling or neglecting logging prevents forensic analysis and detection of unauthorized activity. Storing logs on a secure filesystem prevents exposure or tampering. Proper log management supports non-repudiation and accountability.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: Do not introduce a separate way to start CockroachDB; modify the existing cockroach.service from Control 1.2. 1. Create and harden the log directory: mkdir -p /var/lib/cockroach/logs chown -R cockroach:cockroach /var/lib/cockroach/logs chmod 700 /var/lib/cockroach/logs This aligns with the docs' recommendation to use a separate directory from the main store for logs in cloud / IOPS-sensitive deployments. 2. Add logging configuration to cockroach.service: Edit /etc/systemd/system/cockroach.service (the unit defined in 1.2) and update the existing ExecStart to include a secure logging path. For example: [Service] WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/cockroach ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cockroach start \ --certs-dir=certs \ --store=/var/lib/cockroach \ --log-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/logs \ --advertise-addr=<node address> \ --join=<node1 address>,<node2 address>,<node3 address> \ --cache=.25 \ --max-sql-memory=.25 User=cockroach --log-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/logs is an alias for --log='file-defaults: {dir: /var/lib/cockroach/logs}'. Alternatively, point to a YAML configuration: ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cockroach start \ --certs-dir=certs \ --store=/var/lib/cockroach \ --log-config-file=/etc/cockroach/log-config.yaml \ ... Ensure the YAML uses appropriate file-defaults / file-groups (e.g., dir, file- permissions, max-file-size, max-group-size) consistent with or hardening the documented defaults. Reload and restart: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart cockroach.service 3. Tighten file permissions (if needed): If files were created with looser modes, enforce restrictive permissions: chmod 640 /var/lib/cockroach/logs/*.log If you use a YAML log config, set file-permissions: "0640" (or stricter) in file-defaults or specific file-groups. 4. Validate logging after changes: • Perform any test action such as adding rows, simple query. • Confirm that new entries appear in the appropriate log files (for example, cockroach.log)

check.check-content: Prerequisite: Control 1.2 is implemented and CockroachDB is started only via systemd (e.g., cockroach.service). 1. Verify that CockroachDB logging is enabled and logs are securely stored: For default configurations: cockroach debug check-log-config For custom configured during: Check for explicit logging flags on the running process: Inspect the ExecStart line in the active systemd unit: sudo systemctl cat cockroach.service | grep ExecStart Expected Results: One of the following is true: • The ExecStart line contains --log-dir=<path>, for example: --log-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/logs ( --log-dir=XXX is an alias for --log='file-defaults: {dir: XXX}'). • Or the ExecStart line contains either: o --log-config-file=/path/to/log-config.yaml, or o --log={yaml}. If none of these flags are present, determine the on-disk store directory from the -- store flag (or the default cockroach-data) and infer the logging directory as <store>/logs. For hardened deployments, prefer an explicit log directory separate from the main data store to avoid IOPS contention. 2. Verify the existence and timeliness of log files: Using the identified logging directory (e.g., /cockroach-data/logs or a custom directory such as /var/lib/cockroach/logs), verify that log files exist and have recent modification times, for example: ls -lh /var/lib/cockroach/logs or ls -lh /cockroach-data/logs ( default) tail -n 10 /var/lib/cockroach/logs/cockroach.log With the default logging configuration, expect files such as: • cockroach.log (general / DEV and OPS) • cockroach-security.log (USER_ADMIN, PRIVILEGES) • cockroach-sql-audit.log (SENSITIVE_ACCESS) • cockroach-sql-auth.log (SESSIONS) 3. Verify directory ownership and permissions: Check that the log directory and files are owned by the CockroachDB service account and have restrictive permissions: ls -ld /var/lib/cockroach/logs Expected Results: • Owner: cockroach • Group: cockroach • Mode: drwx------ (700) or more restrictive. The service in Control 1.2 should already be configured to run as User=cockroach Expected Results: • The systemd service's ExecStart line configures logging either via: o --log-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/logs (or another secure path), or o --log-config-file or --log={yaml}, or, if relying on defaults, logs are observed in <store>/logs (for example, /cockroach-data/logs). • Log files such as cockroach.log, cockroach-security.log, and cockroach- sql-audit.log exist in the configured logging directory with recent timestamps. • The log directory is owned by the CockroachDB service account and has permissions of 700 (or stricter). Log files are owned by the same account and have permissions of 640 (or stricter). If any of these checks fail, this is a finding.

Rule.title: Ensure Log Rotation and Retention Settings Are Configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB log rotation and retention must be configured to prevent uncontrolled growth and to preserve an appropriate history window.
