CockroachDB supports per-group rotation parameters that control both individual file size and total group retention. Each log file group can define: • max-file-size - maximum size of an individual log file before a new file is created. • max-group-size - total size (or number of files) to retain before older files are purged. By default, CockroachDB rotates each file at ~10 MiB and keeps about 100 MiB (~10 files) per group.
Rationale: Unbounded log growth poses both reliability and security risks. If log files are not rotated, a busy CockroachDB node could generate extremely large files, potentially exhausting disk space or complicating log review. Proper log rotation ensures: • Predictable and capped disk usage. • Easier log management and review. • Compliance with audit retention policies. • Smaller, segmented logs suitable for archiving or centralization.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Use defaults or define explicit rotation settings: If you do not configure a custom logging YAML, CockroachDB applies defaults of max- file-size: 10MiB and max-group-size: 100MiB to most file groups, which are acceptable for many small-to-medium deployments. To explicitly configure rotation and retention for self-hosted nodes, define or edit a logging configuration YAML, for example: file-defaults: dir: /var/lib/cockroach/logs max-file-size: 10MiB # default per-file size max-group-size: 500MiB # example: increase retention cluster-wide filter: INFO sinks: file-groups: default: # Inherit dir, max-file-size, max-group-size from file-defaults channels: {INFO: [DEV, OPS], WARNING: [HEALTH, STORAGE, SESSIONS, SQL_SCHEMA, USER_ADMIN, PRIVILEGES, SENSITIVE_ACCESS, SQL_EXEC, SQL_PERF, SQL_INTERNAL_PERF, TELEMETRY, KV_DISTRIBUTION]} sql-audit: channels: {INFO: [SENSITIVE_ACCESS]} max-file-size: 20MiB # override if audit volume is high max-group-size: 200MiB buffered-writes: false # typical for security/audit logs auditable: true # when using file-based auditing • file-defaults is the recommended place to set common dir, max-file-size and max-group-size for all file groups, overriding only where necessary. • max-group-size controls total bytes of all log files per group; when exceeded, the oldest files are removed asynchronously. 2. Start nodes with the configuration: Start (or restart) each self-hosted node with the logging configuration: • For nodes started directly with cockroach start, apply the logging configuration as follows: cockroach start \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --store=/var/lib/cockroach \ --log-config-file=/etc/cockroach/logging.yaml Alternatively, you can override rotation parameters inline with the --log flag, for example: cockroach start \ --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs \ --store=/var/lib/cockroach \ --log='file-defaults: {dir: /var/lib/cockroach/logs, max-file-size: 10MiB, max-group-size: 500MiB}' ```[[cockroach start – logging](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/cockroach- start#logging)] • For nodes managed by systemd using cockroachdb.service, add the same -- log or --log-config-file (example: --log-config- file=/etc/cockroach/logging.yaml) flags to the ExecStart line in the service unit and then run: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart securecockroachdb 3. Adjust retention to meet policy: • Set max-group-size (or max-file-count if used) to retain logs for the desired number of days. • Estimate daily log volume to determine appropriate total retention (i.e. In high-traffic deployments, It is recommendded increasing file-defaults.max- group-size to 500MiB or 1GiB to extend log retention). • If a centralized log management system is used, keep only a small local backlog and forward older logs. 4. Verify rotation after changes: After configuration, monitor the log directory over time. You should observe: • New files being created when size thresholds are exceeded. • Oldest files automatically deleted when the total size limit is reached. If this behavior does not occur,: • The YAML syntax (especially indentation and placement under file-defaults and sinks.file-groups). • That nodes were actually started with --log or --log-config-file and not with conflicting flags such as --log-dir alone. 5. Ensure diagnostic bundles can still be collected: Ensure that rotation does not interfere with diagnostic collections. The cockroach debug zip command automatically includes rotated log files. As a best practice, avoid setting max-file-size extremely low (for example, a few kilobytes), as this could create thousands of small files and impact performance or manageability.

check.check-content: 1. Review the active logging configuration: • To view the current logging configuration as applied: Use the following command on a node to display the validated logging configuration: cockroach debug check-log-config if you want to see the default or currently active configuration.* • Alternatively, if you start nodes with a static ( – log config) YAML file: sudo grep -A10 'file-groups:' /etc/cockroach/logging.yaml Verify that each file-groups entry used in production has reasonable values for: • max-file-size • max-group-size 2. Inspect on-disk rotation behavior: Check the node's log directory (by default inferred from the first store directory as cockroach-data/logs, or as customized with file-defaults.dir). ls -lh /var/lib/cockroach/logs du -sh /var/lib/cockroach/logs 3. Check file sizes and count per log group: find /var/lib/cockroach/logs -type f -printf '%p %s\n' \ | sort -k2 -nr | head 4. Confirm rotation behavior via filenames and timestamps: ls -ltr /var/lib/cockroach/logs | tail Expected Results: • EMultiple timestamped files per group (e.g., cockroach.log, cockroach.2025- 10-22T14_10_00Z.log). • File sizes are capped approximately at the configured max-file-size. • The total size of files per group does not exceed max-group-size (The total size of files per group does not exceed ). • No single log file grows indefinitely. If logs exceed expected limits or only a single oversized file exists, rotation is misconfigured - this is a finding.

Rule.title: Ensure Connection Authentication Logging Is Enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB can log client connection attempts, successful logins, authentication failures, and session disconnections through the SESSIONS logging channel. By default, this channel's logging is disabled to minimize overhead on all clusters. Enabling connection and authentication logging ensures that each login event is recorded with details such as the username, client host/IP address, and timestamp for both connection and disconnection events. These settings are controlled by two cluster parameters: • server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled - logs connection open and close events. • server.auth_log.sql_sessions.enabled - logs authentication successes, failures, and session termination. Both parameters must be set to true to enable comprehensive session logging.
Rationale: Tracking who connects to the database, when, and from where is fundamental to security monitoring. Authentication logs provide early visibility into brute-force attempts, misuse of credentials, or anomalous login patterns. They form a crucial audit trail for compliance and incident response.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Enable connection and authentication logging: Use SQL to enable both cluster settings: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> \ -e "SET CLUSTER SETTING server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled = true;" cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> \ -e \"SET CLUSTER SETTING server.auth_log.sql_sessions.enabled = true;\" These settings apply cluster-wide and persist across restarts. 2. Ensure SESSIONS channel is logged to disk With the default logging configuration, the SESSIONS channel is already mapped to cockroach-sql-auth.log via the sql-auth file group. By default, server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled and server.auth_log.sql_sessions.enabled are false, so no connection events are logged. If you use a custom logging YAML, verify that SESSIONS is included in at least one file sink, for example: sinks: file-groups: sql-auth: channels: {INFO: [SESSIONS]} dir: /var/lib/cockroach/logs max-file-size: 10MiB max-group-size: 100MiB buffered-writes: false format: crdb-v2 This ensures SESSIONS events are persisted to disk. Adjust rotation ( max-file-size, max-group-size) in line with Control 3.2. 3. Be aware of performance impact: Cockroach Labs documents that enabling server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled and server.auth_log.sql_sessions.enabled can impact performance because each event incurs a disk write. • Enable both by default on security-sensitive or audited clusters. • On extremely high-throughput clusters, consider sampling or tightening HBA rules while monitoring the performance impact. 4. Integrate with centralized logging (if applicable): • Include cockroach-sql-auth.log (or the custom sink that carries SESSIONS) in your log shipping configuration. • Use the structured fields ( EventType, User, RemoteAddress, Method, Reason) for alerting on repeated failures or suspicious IP ranges.

check.check-content: 1. Verify cluster settings for connection and session authentication logging: cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> \ -e "SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled;" cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> \ -e "SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.auth_log.sql_sessions.enabled;" Expected Results: server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled ------------------------------- true server.auth_log.sql_sessions.enabled ---------------------------- true Both settings must be true for comprehensive logging of connection and authentication events to SESSIONS. 2. Verify that the SESSIONS log file is present and contains recent events: Determine the logging directory (default <store>/logs, for example /var/lib/cockroach/logs). ls -lh /var/lib/cockroach/logs/ tail -n 10 /var/lib/cockroach/logs/cockroach-sql-auth.log In the default configuration, you should see cockroach-sql-auth.log (or rotated variants such as cockroach-sql-auth.2025- …log) tied to the SESSIONS channel. Expected Result : • JSON event entries with EventType such as client_connection_start, client_connection_end, client_authentication_info, client_authentication_ok, client_authentication_failed, and client_session_end. • Fields including User, RemoteAddress, Network, Transport, and timestamps. Example (password failure): ... "EventType":"client_authentication_failed", ... "User":"‹roach›","Detail":"‹password authentication failed for user roach›","Method":"cert -password"} ... "EventType":"client_session_end", ... "RemoteAddress":"‹[::1]:52632›","Duration":... 3. Verify events via system.eventlog: If server.eventlog.enabled is true (default), notable SQL session events are also written into system.eventlog per tenant. cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=<node> \ -e "SELECT timestamp, (info::JSONB)->>'EventType' AS eventtype, info FROM system.eventlog WHERE (info::JSONB)->>'EventType' IN ('client_connection_start', 'client_connection_end', 'client_authentication_failed', 'client_session_end') ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 20;" Presence of recent records for active clients further confirms that connection and authentication events are being captured. 4. Verify inclusion in centralized logging: If you ship logs to a SIEM or log aggregator, confirm that messages from the SESSIONS channel (typically from cockroach-sql-auth.log) are collected. How you query this depends on your logging stack.

Rule.title: Ensure Database Monitoring and Alerting Are in Place
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>A robust monitoring and alerting system must be implemented for CockroachDB to continuously observe the health, performance, and security posture of the database cluster. CockroachDB exposes detailed metrics and events through its internal time- series database and provides a built-in Admin UI (DB Console) for visualization. For comprehensive observability, these metrics should be exported to an external monitoring stack such as Prometheus and Grafana, and alerts should be configured using tools like Alertmanager or equivalent monitoring services. Key aspects include: • Node and Cluster Health: Live node count, replication status, and under- replicated ranges. • Performance Metrics: Throughput, latency, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk). • Security Events: Frequent authentication failures, unusual query volume, or configuration changes. • Backup and Job Status: Ensure scheduled tasks complete successfully. Please find more information here: https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/essential-metrics-self-hosted
Rationale: Continuous monitoring enables early detection of both operational and security anomalies. Metrics and alerts allow administrators to respond proactively to incidents such as node outages, disk exhaustion, performance degradation, or unauthorized activity. Effective monitoring also supports compliance frameworks that require audit log management and system availability oversight.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Integrate with Prometheus and Grafana: Configure Prometheus to scrape metrics from all CockroachDB nodes (default endpoint: http://<node>:8080/_status/vars). Example Prometheus job configuration: scrape_configs: - job_name: 'cockroachdb' scrape_interval: 10s static_configs: - targets: ['node1:8080', 'node2:8080', 'node3:8080'] Import the official CockroachDB Grafana dashboard JSON from Cockroach Labs to visualize performance data. 2. Set Up Alerting: Define alert rules for conditions such as: • Node down or unreachable for >1 minute • Disk capacity <15% • CPU >90% for 10 minutes • Query latency above threshold • Frequent authentication failures; Integrate alerts with notification channels (email, PagerDuty, Slack, etc.). 3. Use and Secure the DB Console: Ensure the Admin UI is enabled and accessible over TLS. Regularly review Metrics and Events pages for anomalies. 4. Centralize Logs and Correlate with Metrics: Forward CockroachDB logs and audit data to your SIEM or log management platform. 5. Establish Routine Checks: Conduct periodic reviews of dashboards and alerts, perform simulated outage drills, and update rules as new risks or features emerge.

check.check-content: Perform the following checks to confirm that monitoring and alerting are properly configured: # 1. Verify that Prometheus or an equivalent collector is scraping CockroachDB metrics # Check the Prometheus configuration for CockroachDB targets: grep "cockroach" /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml # or verify metrics endpoint access directly from a node: curl -s http://<node-host>:8080/_status/vars | head # 2. Verify Grafana dashboards are deployed and show live data # (Log into Grafana at https://<grafana-server>:3000 and confirm CockroachDB panels update) # The official dashboard JSON is available from Cockroach Labs documentation. # 3. Verify alerting rules are configured (Prometheus Alertmanager or equivalent) grep "alert:" /etc/prometheus/alert.rules.yml # Expected rules: node down, high CPU usage, low disk space, replication issues, failed backups, etc. # 4. Verify DB Console (Admin UI) metrics and event logs # Access https://<node>:8080, navigate to: # Metrics → confirm charts update. # Advanced Debug → Events → confirm node join/restart/configuration events appear. # 5. Verify process ownership and alert response procedures # Interview administrators or review documentation confirming that alerts are actively monitored and acted upon. Expected Results: • Metrics endpoint ( /_status/vars) is reachable and producing data. • Grafana dashboards show current activity and historical trends. • Alerting rules exist for critical events (node down, high latency, disk <15%). • Admin UI displays live metrics and events. • A defined process exists for alert response and periodic review. If any of these components are missing or inactive, this is a finding.

Rule.title: Restrict Access Using Host-Based Authentication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB uses a host-based authentication (HBA) configuration to control which SQL connection attempts are allowed to proceed and which authentication methods they may use, based on the originating IP address and the SQL user. HBA rules are expressed in a PostgreSQL-compatible DSL and stored in the server.host_based_authentication.configuration cluster setting; each rule defines a connection type, database scope (currently always all), user, address (IP/CIDR), and authentication method. By configuring this setting, administrators can explicitly restrict inbound SQL connections to approved network ranges and enforce the desired authentication methods per origin, adding an application-layer access-control boundary on top of network-level controls. For hardened deployments, HBA rules should permit connections only from trusted IP addresses or CIDR ranges and then require strong authentication methods such as TLS client certificates (cert / cert-password / cert-scram-sha-256) or SCRAM-SHA-256 (scram-sha-256), depending on organizational policy. Less restrictive methods like password can be allowed where justified, but unauthenticated or trivially authenticated methods such as trust should be avoided in production, and reject should be used as a catch-all deny rule for unintended origins.
Rationale: Restrictive HBA configuration reduces the attack surface by ensuring that only connections from explicitly permitted IP addresses or ranges can reach the authentication stage, even if credentials are compromised. Binding each allowed origin to a strong authentication method, such as certificate-based or SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication, limits downgrade opportunities and helps prevent unauthorized network-based access. Because HBA operates at the SQL layer, it provides an additional defense-in-depth control beyond network firewalls and load balancer rules, and can be used to implement patterns such as "jumpbox-only" access or IP-scoped user rules.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Define explicit whitelisted origins Construct an HBA configuration that lists only authorized IP ranges or hosts. For example: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration = ' TYPE DATABASE USER ADDRESS METHOD host all jump_user 203.0.113.10/32 password host all app_user 198.51.100.0/24 password host all all all reject '; This pattern mirrors the documented approach of whitelisting a jumpbox or application IPs and rejecting all others. 2. Enforce appropriate authentication methods Adjust the METHOD column so that each allowed origin uses an authentication method consistent with organizational policy (for example, cert or scram-sha-256 for human users, cert/cert-scram-sha-256 for service accounts), following the supported methods listed in the documentation. 3. Remove or tighten permissive rules: • Replace overly broad rules (for example, host all all all password) with IP-scoped entries and a final reject rule. • Remove or narrow any rules that grant access from unapproved IP ranges or that permit methods contrary to hardening policy. 4. Apply configuration changes • Set the updated HBA configuration: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration = '<rules>'; • No node restart is required; HBA changes take effect from the cluster setting, but existing sessions will continue using the authentication method under which they were established.

check.check-content: 1. Review HBA configuration for allowed network origins SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration; Expected Results: • Rules explicitly list approved IP addresses or CIDR ranges for client access (for example, a jumpbox /32 or specific app subnets). • A final rule (or equivalent configuration) rejects all other addresses using reject or an IP pattern that effectively denies unintended sources. Fail if: • The configuration is empty or effectively equivalent to host all all all password on self-hosted, which is the default and not hardened. • Broad patterns such as all without a corresponding reject rule allow unvetted origins that violate organizational policy. 2. Verify authentication methods for each origin From the same server.host_based_authentication.configuration output, inspect the METHOD column for each rule. Expected Results: • Strong methods such as cert, cert-password, cert-scram-sha-256, or scram-sha-256 are used where required by policy. • reject is used for disallowed origins. Fail if: • Rules intended to be hardened rely on trust (no authentication) or on weaker methods in contexts where strong methods are mandated by policy (for example, where the Benchmark requires SCRAM-only, but password is still allowed). 3. Verify default-deny behavior Confirm that the effective rule set implements a default-deny stance — for example, by ending with: host all all all reject as shown in hardened examples. Fail if: There is no explicit or effective deny rule for "all other" origins, resulting in unintended access from unlisted networks.

Rule.title: Restrict and Secure Password Authentication
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB self-hosted clusters support several authentication methods for SQL clients, including passwords, SCRAM-SHA-256, TLS client certificates, and others such as GSSAPI/Kerberos (Enterprise), JWT, LDAP/AD and OIDC. For production, Cockroach Labs recommends using TLS client certificates instead of passwords, and provides first-class support for SCRAM-SHA-256 as a stronger password-based mechanism where passwords are still required. In self-hosted environments, operators can further restrict where and how password authentication is used by configuring the HBA rules ( server.host_based_authentication.configuration) and by managing per-user authentication settings via SQL statements such as CREATE USER and ALTER USER. CockroachDB supports SCRAM-SHA-256 for storing and verifying password credentials and provides guidance for enabling SCRAM for new and existing users, including migration from older cleartext/bcrypt formats. Operators can configure the cluster to encrypt new passwords using SCRAM-SHA-256 ( server.user_login.password_encryption = 'scram-sha-256') and allow pre- hashed SCRAM passwords where strict isolation of cleartext credentials is required. For hardened self-hosted deployments, passwords should be minimized and, where necessary, protected with SCRAM-SHA-256 and constrained to specific users and client origins via HBA rules, while the majority of access relies on stronger certificate- based or externally managed authentication mechanisms.
Rationale: Password-based authentication is more susceptible to brute-force attacks, credential reuse, and phishing than certificate-based or federated identity mechanisms. CockroachDB's support for TLS client certificates and SCRAM-SHA-256 enables operators to reduce these risks by preferring certificate-based authentication and, where passwords remain in use, storing them as strong SCRAM hashes instead of weaker or cleartext formats. Enforcing SCRAM-SHA-256 for password credentials and phasing out legacy cleartext/bcrypt formats hardens the cluster against offline cracking and replay attacks, and aligns with CockroachDB's recommendation to migrate existing users to SCRAM. Separating privileged access paths and favoring certificate-based authentication for highly privileged roles (for example, root with TLS client certificates) provides stronger cryptographic guarantees and reduces reliance on reusable secrets for critical administration tasks. Restricting where password authentication is allowed — via both user configuration and HBA rules — helps ensure that password-based logins are tightly controlled, strongly hashed, and limited in scope, contributing to a defense-in-depth posture for self-hosted clusters.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Enable SCRAM-SHA-256 for new passwords Configure the cluster to use SCRAM-SHA-256 for all newly set passwords: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.user_login.password_encryption = 'scram-sha-256'; This ensures that any CREATE USER ... WITH PASSWORD or ALTER USER ... WITH PASSWORD operations store SCRAM-SHA-256 hashes. 2. Migrate existing users to SCRAM-SHA-256 If legacy/bcrypt hashes exist and migration is desired: • For eventual migration: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.user_login.upgrade_bcrypt_stored_passwords_to_scram.enabled = true; • For immediate migration, rotate passwords: ALTER USER {user} WITH PASSWORD '{new_password}'; This writes a SCRAM-SHA-256 hash if server.user_login.password_encryption = 'scram-sha-256'. 3. Optionally implement strict isolation of cleartext credentials For environments that require full separation of cleartext password handling: • Enable acceptance of pre-computed SCRAM hashes: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.user_login.store_client_pre_hashed_passwords.enabled = true; • Configure HBA to allow only scram-sha-256 and/or cert-scram-sha-256, and remove password / cert-password from allowed methods: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration = ' TYPE DATABASE USER ADDRESS METHOD host all app_user all scram-sha-256 host all all all reject '; Generate SCRAM hashes externally and use them directly in CREATE USER / ALTER USER statements as documented. 4. Tighten HBA rules around password usage Replace broad password-based rules with IP-scoped and user-scoped entries that use scram-sha-256 where passwords are allowed and reject for other cases, following the secure HBA examples.

check.check-content: 1. Review SQL users and hashed password formats • List users: SHOW USERS; This shows usernames and role memberships To inspect stored password hashes and infer whether SCRAM-SHA-256 is used: SET bytea_output = 'escape'; SELECT username, "hashedPassword" FROM system.users WHERE "hashedPassword" IS NOT NULL; SCRAM-SHA-256 hashes appear with the SCRAM-SHA-256$... prefix when decoded from hex Expected Results (for hardened deployments): • Most privileged and application accounts either: o Do not have a password (and use certificate or other non-password auth), or o Have SCRAM-SHA-256 hashes, not legacy/bcrypt formats. • No unexpected users with password hashes exist beyond those intended by policy. Fail if: • Many or all users have legacy non-SCRAM hashes, contrary to cluster policy where SCRAM is required. • Users that should rely on certificate-based or external authentication still have local password hashes, against policy. 2. Verify cluster settings enforce SCRAM-SHA-256 for new/updated passwords Check the password encryption mode: SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.user_login.password_encryption; Expected Results: • scram-sha-256 for hardened self-hosted deployments. Optionally, confirm automatic migration of bcrypt passwords to SCRAM (if enabled by policy): SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.user_login.upgrade_bcrypt_stored_passwords_to_scram.enabled; Expected Results (if migration is desired): • true in v22.2+ to automatically upgrade legacy bcrypt hashes on first login. Fail if: • server.user_login.password_encryption is not set to scram-sha-256 where policy requires SCRAM. • Automatic upgrade settings conflict with the organization's migration strategy. 3. Review HBA configuration for password-based methods Display HBA: SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration; Inspect METHOD values for rules that allow password-based authentication, such as password or scram-sha-256. Expected Results: • Password-based methods appear only where explicitly intended (for example, limited user/IP combinations). • No trust entries are used in hardened self-hosted production. Fail if: • Broad rules (for example, host all all all password) permit password authentication from unbounded origins against policy. • trust or other unauthenticated methods appear in production HBA.

Rule.title: Secure the root User and Administrative Roles
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The root user in CockroachDB has unrestricted administrative privileges across the entire cluster. Because compromise of root grants full control, its use must be tightly restricted and secured. The root account should authenticate exclusively with TLS client certificates (mTLS), and password authentication must be disabled. Access to root should be limited to hardened administrative hosts (e.g., jump boxes/bastion hosts) via host-based access rules. The root user must not be used for day-to-day operations, routine queries, application access, or automated scripts; instead, operational tasks should be performed using delegated roles with least privilege.
Rationale: The root account is a high-value target for attackers. Certificate-based authentication provides significantly stronger protection than passwords because it requires possession of a private key rather than a reusable secret. Preventing password authentication for root, restricting where root can log in from, and enforcing strict operational separation reduces the risk of cluster-wide compromise. Delegating password fallback to a separate emergency user (Control 1.3) preserves recoverability without weakening root security.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Enforce certificate-only authentication for root Update the HBA configuration to allow only certificate-based methods: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration = ' TYPE DATABASE USER ADDRESS METHOD host all root <jumpbox-cidr> cert host all root all reject '; Replace <jumpbox-cidr> with your actual admin network. 2. Restrict root usage operationally • Replace script usage with least-privilege service accounts. • Ensure applications do not use root. • Use root only for tasks requiring full administrative privilege.

check.check-content: 1. Verify root authentication requires TLS client certificates (mTLS): Check HBA configuration: SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.host_based_authentication.configuration; Expected Results: • Entries for root use methods such as cert or cert-*. • No password-based or unauthenticated method ( password, scram-sha-256, trust) appears for root. • root access restricted to specific jump-box IP addresses or CIDR blocks. • No wildcard or universal access (e.g., all, 0.0.0.0/0,::/0). Fail if: • Any rule allows root to authenticate using a password. • Any rule allows root without certificate authentication. • root can connect from any IP or a broad range outside approved admin hosts. 2. Verify root is not used for routine or application operations If audit logs are enabled: cockroach sql --execute=" SELECT timestamp, eventType, reportingID FROM system.eventlog WHERE info LIKE '%root%'; " Fail if: • root is used frequently by applications or scripts. • Routine operations are performed using root instead of delegated roles.

Rule.title: Centralize and Standardize User Management
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Self-hosted CockroachDB clusters should maintain consistent and centralized management of database user identities to ensure secure, controlled, and predictable access. CockroachDB supports several external authentication systems — such as OIDC, GSSAPI/Kerberos, and LDAP — but organizations may also centralize identity management by standardizing how CockroachDB accounts are created, assigned roles, and deprovisioned. Centralizing user lifecycle processes reduces the risk of unmanaged or orphaned accounts and ensures that authentication and authorization policies are applied consistently across environments. When possible, administrators should prefer certificate-based authentication or integrate CockroachDB with an external identity provider to unify identity governance.
Rationale: Decentralized or ad-hoc management of CockroachDB user accounts increases the likelihood of misaligned privileges, stale accounts, and unauthorized access. A centralized user management process — whether implemented operationally or via integration with an external directory — improves governance, auditability, and consistency. Even without full IdP integration, standardizing user provisioning, modification, and deprovisioning across self-hosted clusters strengthens security posture.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Establish a centralized user management process Document and enforce: • Account creation approval • Standardized role/privilege assignment • Required justification for role elevation • Timely account deprovisioning 2. Remove orphaned or unauthorized accounts DROP USER <username>; Only after confirming the user is no longer required and privileges are reassigned as needed. Encourage certificate-based authentication for administrators and service accounts. 3. (Optional) Integrate an external identity provider If suitable for the environment, configure CockroachDB with: • OIDC • GSSAPI/Kerberos • LDAP To unify database identities with organizational IAM.

check.check-content: 1. Review user lifecycle documentation or practices: Verify administrators follow a defined user management workflow including: • Approval required for account creation • Standard role assignment rules • Prompt deprovisioning of users who no longer require access Fail if: • No documented or enforced process exists • Users remain active after leaving the organization or after their access is no longer needed 2. Review CockroachDB users for orphaned or unused accounts: Run: SHOW USERS; Expected Results: • Only current, authorized users exist • No stale, unused, or orphaned accounts appear Fail if: • Accounts exist that do not correspond to active personnel or services 3. Verify consistent authentication methods Check whether users have local password hashes (meaning they rely on password auth) or no hash (meaning certificate/IdP authentication): SELECT username, (hashedPassword != '\x') AS has_password FROM system.users; Interpretation: • has_password = false → user authenticates via certificates or external identity • has_password = true → user authenticates using a password Fail if: • Authentication methods vary without policy • Users authenticate in ways that contradict organizational standards • Users expected to use certificates still have password hashes 4. If external identity integration is used, verify configuration: (Required only if the organization has deployed external auth.) Confirm that: • OIDC configuration is valid • Kerberos/GSSAPI or LDAP settings are correct • Authentication flows align with organizational identity policies

Rule.title: Ensure Backups Are Encrypted Using an External Method
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In self-hosted CockroachDB deployments, the Encryption-at-Rest (EAR) feature encrypts only the node's local on-disk data, including SSTables, write-ahead logs (WAL), and temporary files. EAR does not encrypt backup files created using the BACKUP statement. By default, backups generated by CockroachDB are written as plaintext objects to the configured backup destination unless an explicit backup encryption mechanism is enabled. As a result, backup data may be exposed if the storage location is accessed by unauthorized users. To protect backup data, organizations must apply separate encryption for all backup files using one or more of the following CockroachDB-supported methods: • Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) - based encryption (recommended), using AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or Azure Key Vault to encrypt a randomly generated data-encryption key for each backup. • AES-256 passphrase-based encryption, which encrypts backup manifests and data files using a key derived from a strong passphrase. • Storage-provider encryption, where the destination storage system enforces encryption at rest (for example, Amazon S3 server-side encryption, Google Cloud Storage default encryption or CMEK, or Azure Storage Service Encryption).
Rationale: Backup files typically contain a complete copy of the database, including sensitive or regulated information. Because CockroachDB's EAR feature does not protect backup objects, leaving backups unencrypted exposes organizations to risks such as: • Compromise of cloud storage buckets or local filesystems • Misconfigured access control lists (ACLs) or IAM policies • Exposure through snapshots or removable media • Insider access or credential theft Using explicit backup encryption — either at the SQL level (passphrase or KMS) or enforced at the storage layer — ensures that backup data remains confidential even if the backup storage location is compromised. This provides cryptographic separation between live database storage and backup data and aligns with regulatory requirements for encryption of data at rest.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: Option 1 - Enable AES-256 Passphrase-Based Backup Encryption Configure backups to use passphrase-based encryption: BACKUP DATABASE <db> INTO 's3://bucket/path?AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...&AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...' WITH encryption_passphrase = '<strong-passphrase>'; Use an external secret manager (e.g., Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) to store the passphrase (not documented in CockroachDB, but strongly recommended operationally). Option 2 — Use Cloud KMS - managed encryption (recommended) Use the kms option so that CockroachDB encrypts each backup with a random 256-bit key, which is then encrypted by the cloud KMS. Example — AWS KMS: BACKUP INTO 's3://{BUCKET NAME}?AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID={KEY ID}&AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY={SECRET ACCESS KEY}' WITH kms = 'aws:///{key}?AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID={KEY ID}&AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY={SECRET ACCESS KEY}&REGION=us-east-1'; Example — GCP KMS: BACKUP INTO 'gs://{BUCKET NAME}?AUTH=specified&CREDENTIALS={ENCODED KEY}' WITH kms = 'gs:///projects/{project name}/locations/us- east1/keyRings/{key ring name}/cryptoKeys/{key name}?AUTH=specified&CREDENTIALS={encoded key}'; Example — AZURE KMS: BACKUP INTO 'azure-blob://{container name}?AUTH=specified&AZURE_ACCOUNT_NAME={account name}&AZURE_CLIENT_ID={client ID}&AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET={client secret}&AZURE_TENANT_ID={tenant ID}' WITH kms = 'azure-kms:///{key}/{key version}?AZURE_TENANT_ID={tenant ID}&AZURE_CLIENT_ID={client ID}&AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET={client secret}&AZURE_VAULT_NAME={key vault name}'; The same kms URI(s) must be supplied for RESTORE and SHOW BACKUP to decrypt the backup. Option 3 — Enforce encryption at the storage layer If you do not use SQL-level backup encryption: • Configure S3, GCS, or Azure Blob Storage to require server-side encryption for all objects. • Ensure bucket/container policies block uploads without encryption. CockroachDB will then write plaintext backup objects that are encrypted at rest by the storage provider.

check.check-content: 1. Identify recent CockroachDB backups • Artifact-level view : SHOW BACKUPS IN 's3://bucket/path?AUTH=...'; SHOW BACKUP FROM '<subdir>' IN 's3://bucket/path?AUTH=...'; • Job-level view : SELECT * FROM system.jobs WHERE job_type = 'BACKUP' ORDER BY created DESC; Warning (unsafe internals, audit-only): This step uses the system.jobs table behind the allow_unsafe_internals gate and is not a supported production API for general use . Treat it strictly as a break-glass operation during periodic audits, run only in a dedicated admin session by authorized operators. Do not expose this query or allow_unsafe_internals = true to application workloads or end users, and end the session (or reset allow_unsafe_internals to off) immediately after the check . SET allow_unsafe_internals = false; • If you need history beyond the jobs retention window, there is no long-term source in SQL; you need exported logs / observability (e.g., recovery_event in eventlog, log shipping to SIEM) to prove older backups were taken. 2. Inspect backup job options for encryption For each backup job, inspect its details (for example, using SHOW JOB job_id or equivalent) and verify whether one of the following options is present: • encryption_passphrase • kms = ... If neither option appears and storage-layer encryption is not being used (see Step 3), record a finding. 3. Validate destination storage encryption Using cloud or storage tooling outside of CockroachDB, verify encryption at rest is enforced for the backup destination: • AWS S3: Confirm server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) is enabled. • Google Cloud Storage: Confirm default encryption or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are configured. • Azure Blob Storage: Confirm Storage Service Encryption is enabled. If backups are written to a local filesystem, verify that filesystem-level or external encryption is enabled using operating system or platform tooling. If encryption is not enforced at the storage layer, record a finding. 4. Verify secure handling of passphrases and keys Confirm that backup encryption_passphrase or KMS credentials are not stored in plaintext within: • Shell scripts • Systemd unit files • Application source code • CI/CD pipelines • Logs or configuration files Secrets should be stored in an approved secret-management solution.

Rule.title: Periodically Test Backup Recovery Procedures
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Self-hosted CockroachDB deployments must regularly test backup recovery procedures to ensure that backups can be successfully restored, data integrity is preserved, and security controls remain effective during restoration. CockroachDB provides multiple backup and restore features, including full and incremental backups, encrypted backups, and backup validation tools. These features allow you to verify that stored backups are restorable without always performing a full restore. While creating backups (including encrypted backups) is critical, backups that are never tested may be unusable due to corruption, misconfiguration, missing encryption keys, expired credentials, or incorrect recovery procedures. Periodic restore testing validates that: • Backup files are complete and readable (for example, via SHOW BACKUP ... WITH check_files or RESTORE ... WITH schema_only, verify_backup_table_data). • Encryption mechanisms (passphrase or KMS) function correctly during restore when using encrypted backups. • Required credentials and permissions to access external/cloud storage are available and functional. • Restore procedures are documented, repeatable, and effective. Restore testing must be performed in a non-production environment (for example, an empty or dedicated test cluster) to avoid impacting live workloads and to prevent accidental data exposure. schema_only restores and validation restores can be run on such test clusters and then dropped after validation.
Rationale: Backups that cannot be restored are operationally equivalent to having no backups at all. CockroachDB provides tools to take and restore full and incremental backups, including encrypted backups, and to validate that backups are restorable. Common failure scenarios include: • Lost or inaccessible encryption passphrases or KMS keys required to restore encrypted backups. • Undocumented or untested recovery steps. • Corrupted or incomplete backup artifacts (for example, missing SST files in cloud storage). Regular restore testing using CockroachDB's validation and restore mechanisms ensures that: • Recovery time objectives (RTOs) defined in the disaster recovery strategy are achievable in practice. • Data integrity is preserved end-to-end by confirming that schemas and data can be restored and, where applicable, that table data files are present and uncorrupted. • Encryption and access controls remain enforced during recovery when using encrypted backups. • Organizations are prepared for real incident response scenarios, including ransomware or other disaster events. Testing recovery procedures is a fundamental resilience practice and is aligned with CockroachDB's disaster recovery and data resilience guidance.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Define a restore testing schedule Establish a policy requiring restore or backup validation testing at a regular cadence and after key changes, such as: • Changes to backup configuration or destinations. • Changes to backup encryption (for example, enabling encrypted backups or changing KMS configuration). • KMS key rotation or changes to encryption keys. • IAM or credential changes affecting access to backup storage or KMS. • Major CockroachDB version upgrades that may affect backup/restore compatibility. 2. Perform restore tests in a non-production environment Restore or validate backups into a dedicated test cluster or isolated environment using documented procedures: • Primary DR validation (recommended): Run a normal RESTORE (cluster, database, or table, as appropriate) into a real CockroachDB cluster (non-production) and validate that: o The cluster can be provisioned or scaled for recovery. o Restored objects are present and accessible. o Representative application queries run successfully against the restored data. • Supplementary / faster validation between full DR tests (optional): o For schema validation and credential checks, use: RESTORE ... WITH schema_only; on an empty or test cluster to validate backup existence, storage/KMS credentials, and schema/version compatibility. o Where required for additional assurance or compliance, use: RESTORE ... WITH schema_only, verify_backup_table_data; to read and checksum table data from backup storage without writing it to disk. This is a validation/debugging tool and does not replace periodic full RESTORE tests into a real cluster. • For encrypted backups, ensure restore commands include the correct KMS or passphrase configuration. After validation, drop the restored database or destroy the test cluster to return the environment to its pre-test state. 3. Validate data integrity After restoration or validation: • Verify that database objects (databases, tables, schemas) are present using standard SQL inspection (for example, SHOW TABLES). • Run basic queries to confirm data accessibility when performing a full restore test. • Confirm schema and metadata integrity (for example, that table definitions match expectations). • Where applicable, rely on verify_backup_table_data to ensure that table data files are present and uncorrupted. 4. Document and remediate failures If restore testing or backup validation reveals failures: • Update documentation and automation (runbooks, scripts, or scheduled jobs) to reflect correct restore and validation procedures. • Correct permission, connectivity, or encryption issues (for example, missing KMS permissions or incorrect storage URIs). • Re-run restore or validation tests until successful. • Maintain records of restore tests and outcomes, including timestamps, scope (cluster/database/table), and any issues discovered and resolved.

check.check-content: 1. Verify existence of documented restore procedures Confirm that the organization maintains documented procedures covering: • Where CockroachDB backups are stored (for example, S3, GCS, Azure Blob, or other supported cloud storage). • How to restore backups, including: o Use of RESTORE for full-cluster, database, or table restores into a non-production CockroachDB cluster (for example, a dedicated DR/test cluster). o Steps to provision or scale a recovery cluster (infrastructure, networking, access control) and restore into it, so that DR procedures exercise real-world operational workflows (not just validation options). • Use of backup validation options (for testing/debug only), including: o Use of RESTORE ... WITH schema_only as a fast validation / debugging tool to confirm: ▪ Storage credentials and IAM are correct. ▪ Backups exist and are discoverable. ▪ Basic schema and version compatibility. o Optional use of RESTORE ... WITH schema_only, verify_backup_table_data only where required for additional assurance or compliance (for example, to checksum table data files in backup storage). Note that this option: ▪ Must always be used together with schema_only. ▪ Is primarily a validation aid, and is not a substitute for a full restore into a real CockroachDB cluster. • How to restore encrypted backups, including: o Required kms configuration (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) or o Required encryption_passphrase usage. • Required credentials and permissions to access backup storage and KMS. • Validation steps after restore (for example, checking schemas, running queries, or using backup validation options) If no documented restore procedure exists -> Finding 2. Verify restore testing frequency Review operational records, tickets, or logs to confirm that restore tests or backup validation operations are performed on a defined schedule (for example, quarterly, bi- annually, or after major changes). Evidence may include: • Change records or DR test reports referencing RESTORE or SHOW BACKUP ... WITH check_files. • Runbooks or automation with execution timestamps for validation restores (for example, schema_only or verify_backup_table_data restores). • CI/CD or automation logs showing periodic backup validation or test restores. • Monitoring or observability records for backup and restore jobs. If restore testing is ad- hoc or never performed → Finding. 3. Validate successful restore execution Confirm that at least one recent restore or validation test was successfully completed in a non-production environment, including: • Successful access to backup storage and reading of backup files (for example, via SHOW BACKUP ... WITH check_files or a validation restore). • Successful cluster, database, or table restore or validation restore, such as: o RESTORE ... WITH schema_only to validate schema. o RESTORE ... WITH schema_only, verify_backup_table_data to validate that table data files are present and uncorrupted. • Verification that restored objects (schemas and, where applicable, data) are accessible in the test environment. For encrypted backups, confirm that restore tests used the correct encryption configuration: • WITH kms = 'kms://...' (or equivalent) for KMS-encrypted backups, or • WITH encryption_passphrase = '...' for passphrase-encrypted backups. Failure to restore or validate encrypted backups → Finding. 4. Validate post-restore security controls After restore testing, verify that: • Restored data remains protected according to the organization's encryption-at- rest configuration (for example, if encryption at rest is enabled on the test cluster, it remains enabled after restore). • Access controls (SQL users/roles and network controls) are correctly applied in the test environment and do not expose restored data beyond intended scope. • Temporary credentials or secrets used during testing (for example, temporary cloud storage keys or KMS credentials) are revoked or rotated according to organizational policy. If security controls are bypassed or weakened during restore → Finding.

Rule.title: Control Key Data Usage for Multi-Region Clusters with Data Localization Restrictions
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In self-hosted CockroachDB multi-region clusters, organizations must ensure that Personally Identifiable Information (PII) or other regulated data is not used as part of primary key constraints or secondary indexes. In CockroachDB, primary keys define the primary index, and primary key columns are implicitly included in all secondary indexes. When a column is included in a primary key or index, its values are: 1. Stored in index keyspace entries as part of the primary or secondary index. 2. Implicitly included in secondary indexes when part of the primary key. 3. Distributed and replicated across the cluster for query routing and fault tolerance, including across regions in multi-region deployments. As a result, placing PII fields (such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, national identifiers, or other sensitive attributes) into primary keys or secondary indexes can cause unintentional cross-region data replication, potentially conflicting with data localization, residency, or sovereignty requirements. CockroachDB's data domiciling and multi-region features (for example, REGIONAL BY ROW, super regions, and placement controls) are designed to help keep data within specific geographic boundaries, but indexed columns are still part of the distributed key- value and index structures. To comply with data localization restrictions, organizations should ensure that PII fields are stored only as non-indexed columns where possible, and that primary keys and indexes use non-sensitive surrogate identifiers. CockroachDB documentation recommends using UUIDs or composite keys with well-distributed, non-sensitive columns as primary keys, and warns about the implications of primary key design on data distribution.
Rationale: CockroachDB's distributed architecture prioritizes availability and low-latency access by automatically sharding and replicating data, including index structures, across nodes and regions. While this behavior is desirable for performance and resilience, it has implications for sensitive data: • Primary key values are embedded in the primary index and implicitly included in all secondary indexes. • Secondary indexes store indexed column values and primary key columns, which are distributed across the cluster. • In multi-region deployments, index data participates in the same replication and placement mechanisms as other data, and may be present in multiple regions for availability and latency. If PII is used in keys or indexes, it may: • Be stored or replicated in regions where it is not intended to reside, complicating compliance with GDPR, CCPA, or other data residency regulations. • Be exposed to administrators or systems in other jurisdictions that have access to those regions. • Make it harder to enforce strict data localization using features like super regions or placement restrictions, because indexed values are part of the distributed keyspace. By using surrogate keys (for example, UUIDs) and restricting PII to non-indexed columns, organizations can: 1. Follow CockroachDB's primary key best practices (for example, using UUIDs for single-column primary keys). 2. Maintain CockroachDB's performance and availability benefits. 3. Better align with data domiciling and data sovereignty requirements by limiting where sensitive values appear in the distributed keyspace.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Replace PII-based keys with surrogate keys Refactor schemas so that primary keys use surrogate identifiers instead of PII. CockroachDB recommends: • Using UUID-typed columns with default values generated by gen_random_uuid() for single-column primary keys. • Using composite primary keys where the leading column is a well-distributed, non-sensitive identifier. Ensure PII columns are stored as regular, non-indexed fields where possible. Schema changes may require: • Creating a new surrogate key column. • Updating application code to reference the surrogate key. • Using ALTER TABLE ... ALTER PRIMARY KEY to change the primary key definition (not explicitly covered in the provided sources, but implied by CockroachD's support for primary key changes). 2. Remove or redesign PII-based secondary indexes Where indexing on PII is not strictly required: • Drop secondary indexes containing PII columns using DROP INDEX. • Replace them with indexes on non-sensitive identifiers (for example, surrogate keys) that can still support required query patterns. If indexing on PII is required for business reasons: • Document the justification and obtain compliance or legal approval. • Where possible, restrict table locality and data placement using multi-region features (for example, REGIONAL BY ROW plus super regions or placement controls) so that PII-bearing indexes are domiciled within the required geographic boundary. 3. Validate data locality after changes After schema changes: • Verify table locality settings using SHOW CREATE TABLE and database region configuration ( ALTER DATABASE ... PRIMARY REGION, ADD REGION, ADD SUPER REGION). • Confirm that PII columns are not part of primary keys or secondary indexes by re-running SHOW CREATE TABLE and SHOW INDEXES FROM <table_name>. • Re-test application queries to ensure functionality and performance are preserved, adjusting query patterns to use surrogate keys where necessary. • For data domiciling scenarios, verify that regional placement (for example, REGIONAL BY ROW with crdb_region, super regions) still enforces the intended residency boundaries.

check.check-content: 1. Identify multi-region configuration Confirm that the CockroachDB cluster is configured for multi-region deployment. Evidence may include: • Databases configured with PRIMARY REGION and additional REGION entries. • Use of table locality settings such as LOCALITY REGIONAL BY TABLE, LOCALITY REGIONAL BY ROW, or LOCALITY GLOBAL. • Use of super regions or placement controls for data domiciling. If the cluster is single-region only and not using multi-region abstractions, this control may be marked Not Applicable. 2. Identify tables containing PII Review database schemas, data classification inventories, or application documentation to identify tables containing PII or regulated data. CockroachDB does not automatically classify PII, so this step relies on organizational data classification. Common examples include columns such as: • Name, email address, phone number. • National ID numbers. • Customer identifiers tied to real individuals. • Account numbers associated with personal data. If no inventory exists, auditors may need to sample schemas and consult application owners. 3. Review primary key definitions Inspect table definitions to identify whether PII fields are included in primary keys. Use: SHOW CREATE TABLE <table_name>; Review the PRIMARY KEY clause in the CREATE TABLE statement. If any PII column appears in the PRIMARY KEY definition -> Finding. 4. Review secondary indexes List indexes for tables containing PII: SHOW INDEXES FROM <table_name>; The SHOW INDEX output lists each index and its columns, including implicitly included primary key columns. Finding if: • Any PII column is included as an indexed column in a secondary index (that is, appears with s toring = false and implicit = false for that index). • PII appears as part of the primary key and therefore is implicitly included in all secondary indexes ( implicit = true for that column in secondary indexes). 5. Validate use of surrogate identifiers Confirm that: • Primary keys use non-sensitive surrogate identifiers (for example, UUIDs generated with gen_random_uuid() or other non-PII identifiers), consistent with CockroachDB primary key best practices. • PII columns are stored as non-indexed attributes unless explicitly required for lawful and documented reasons (for example, regulatory or business requirements that have been reviewed and approved). • Where PII must be indexed, table locality and data domiciling configurations (for example, REGIONAL BY ROW plus super regions) are used to constrain where that data is stored and replicated

Rule.title: Ensure Certificate File Permissions and Validity
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>While Control 1.3 ensures the cluster operates with TLS enabled, this control focuses on the security and maintenance of the certificate files residing on the node's file system. Critical security artifacts, specifically private keys ( node.key, client.root.key), must be protected with strict OS-level file permissions to prevent unauthorized local users from reading the keys. Additionally, certificates must be actively monitored for validity periods to prevent outages caused by expiration.
Rationale: If a private key file on the disk is improperly secured and world-readable (e.g., chmod 644 or 777), a local attacker on the host system can copy the key, leading to a direct compromise of the private key. This compromises the confidentiality of the system, potentially allowing the attacker to decrypt captured network traffic. Enforcing strict OS- level file permissions (0600) ensures that only the dedicated database user can read the keys, significantly reducing the likelihood of a private key compromise. Furthermore, failing to monitor certificate expiration leads to sudden cluster unavailability when the certificates become invalid and rotation is neglected.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Restrict Private Key Permissions: If keys are found to be too open, lock them down immediately. chmod 600 /var/lib/cockroach/certs/*.key 2. Correct Ownership: Ensure the directory and files are owned by the specific CockroachDB user. chown -R cockroach:cockroach /var/lib/cockroach/certs 3. Renew Expiring Certificates: If openssl indicates the certificate is expired or near expiration: • Generate new certificates on your secure CA workstation (as defined in Control 1.3 Remediation). • Upload them to /var/lib/cockroach/certs on the node. • Reload the certificates by sending a SIGHUP to the process: pkill -SIGHUP cockroach

check.check-content: 1. Verify Private Key Permissions: Run the following command to check permissions for all .key files in the certificate directory.: ls -l /var/lib/cockroach/certs/*.key Expected Results: • Permissions must be -rw------- (600) or -r-------- (400). • Owner must be the database user (e.g., cockroach). Findings: Mark as failed if permissions allow Group or Others to read/write (e.g., -rw- r--r--). 2. Verify Certificate Permissions: Run the following command to check permissions for.crt files: ls -l /var/lib/cockroach/certs/*.crt Expected Results: • Permissions should be -rw-r--r-- (644). • Owner must be the database user (e.g., cockroach). 3. Verify Certificate Expiration: Check the expiration date of the current node certificate. openssl x509 -in /var/lib/cockroach/certs/node.crt -noout -enddate Expected Results: • The output date must be in the future.

Rule.title: Ensure local connections via UNIX domain sockets are configured correctly
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>UNIX domain sockets provide secure local inter-process communication for database connections on the same host. When combined with certificate-based authentication (see section 6.0), UNIX domain sockets offer the most secure mechanism for local database access. For matching UNIX usernames, certificate-less authentication via UNIX domain sockets can provide secure local access without requiring certificate management, though certificate-based authentication is still recommended for maximum security. UNIX domain sockets eliminate network-based attack vectors and provide file system- level access controls. The socket file location, permissions, and authentication methods should be properly configured to prevent unauthorized local access.
Rationale: UNIX domain sockets provide several security advantages for local connections: • No network exposure or attack surface • File system-level access controls • Better performance than TCP/IP for local connections • Integration with UNIX user authentication • Reduced complexity for local administrative tasks</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: Prerequisites: Complete certificate infrastructure setup as described in section 6.0. 1. Configure UNIX Domain Socket Location # Start CockroachDB with custom socket directory cockroach start \ --certs-dir=certs \ --store=node1 \ --listen-addr=localhost:26257 \ --socket-dir=/var/run/cockroach \ --http-addr=localhost:8080 # Ensure socket directory has appropriate permissions mkdir -p /var/run/cockroach chown cockroach:cockroach /var/run/cockroach chmod 755 /var/run/cockroach 2. Create Client Certificates for Local Users # Create database user cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=/tmp --execute="CREATE USER localuser;" # Create client certificate for local user cockroach cert create-client localuser --certs-dir=certs --ca-key=ca- key/ca.key # Create user-specific certificate directory mkdir -p /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs cp certs/ca.crt /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs/ cp certs/client.localuser.crt /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs/ cp certs/client.localuser.key /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs/ # Set appropriate permissions chown -R localuser:localuser /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs chmod 700 /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs chmod 600 /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs/client.localuser.key chmod 644 /home/localuser/.cockroach-certs/*.crt 3. Test Local Authentication # Test as root user cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=/tmp --user=root # Test as regular user su - localuser cockroach sql --certs-dir=/home/localuser/.cockroach-certs --host=/tmp -- user=localuser 4. Security Hardening # Remove world permissions from socket if needed (depends on use case) # Note: This may prevent legitimate access by other users chmod 660 /tmp/.s.PGSQL.26257 # For production, consider dedicated socket directory mkdir -p /var/lib/cockroach/sockets chown cockroach:cockroach /var/lib/cockroach/sockets chmod 750 /var/lib/cockroach/sockets

check.check-content: Prerequisites: Ensure certificate infrastructure is properly configured (see section 6.0). Verify that UNIX domain socket connections work with certificate authentication: # Test local connection via UNIX domain socket with certificates cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=/tmp --user=root root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> Test UNIX domain socket path configuration: # Check default socket location ls -la /tmp/.s.PGSQL.26257 srwxrwxrwx 1 cockroach cockroach 0 [date] /tmp/.s.PGSQL.26257 # Test connection with explicit socket directory cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=/var/run/cockroach --user=root root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> Verify that insecure connections are rejected: # Attempt insecure connection via UNIX socket cockroach sql --insecure --host=/tmp --user=root ERROR: server is not running in insecure mode, must use certificates Verify socket file permissions and ownership: # Check socket file permissions ls -la /tmp/.s.PGSQL.* srwxrwxrwx 1 cockroach cockroach 0 [date] /tmp/.s.PGSQL.26257 # Check socket directory permissions ls -ld /tmp drwxrwxrwt 10 root root 4096 [date] /tmp Test user-specific certificate authentication: # Test with user-specific certificates su - user1 cockroach sql --certs-dir=/home/user1/certs --host=/tmp --user=user1 user1@localhost:26257/defaultdb>

Rule.title: Ensure remote connections via TCP/IP sockets are configured correctly
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>TCP/IP connections enable remote access to CockroachDB clusters across networks. CockroachDB supports multiple authentication methods for remote connections, with certificate-based authentication being the most secure option. All TCP/IP connections must use TLS encryption to protect data in transit. Remote connection security depends on proper network configuration, authentication method selection, and TLS settings. Certificate-based authentication is strongly recommended for production environments as it provides mutual TLS authentication and eliminates password-based attack vectors. Supported authentication methods for remote connections include: • Certificate-based authentication: Uses client certificates signed by the cluster's CA (recommended) • Password authentication: Username and password over TLS • GSSAPI/Kerberos: For enterprise environments with existing Kerberos infrastructure • OIDC/JWT: For integration with identity providers
Rationale: Secure remote connections are essential for: • Distributed cluster administration • Application connectivity from remote hosts • Multi-tier architecture security • Compliance with data protection requirements • Prevention of network-based attacks</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: Prerequisites: Complete certificate infrastructure setup as described in section 6.0. 1. Configure Server for Remote Access # Start CockroachDB listening on appropriate network interfaces cockroach start \ --certs-dir=certs \ --store=node1 \ --listen-addr=0.0.0.0:26257 \ --advertise-addr=database-server:26257 \ --http-addr=0.0.0.0:8080 \ --join=database-server:26257 # For multi-node clusters, configure each node cockroach start \ --certs-dir=certs \ --store=node2 \ --listen-addr=0.0.0.0:26257 \ --advertise-addr=db2.example.com:26257 \ --http-addr=0.0.0.0:8080 \ --join=db1.example.com:26257,db2.example.com:26257,db3.example.com:26257 2. Create Remote Users and Certificates -- Create users for remote access CREATE USER appuser; CREATE USER backupuser; CREATE USER monitoruser; -- For password-based authentication, set passwords ALTER USER appuser WITH PASSWORD 'strong_app_password'; ALTER USER monitoruser WITH PASSWORD 'strong_monitor_password'; -- Grant appropriate privileges GRANT ALL ON DATABASE myapp TO appuser; GRANT SELECT ON DATABASE myapp TO monitoruser; GRANT ALL ON DATABASE *.* TO backupuser; 3. Generate and Distribute Client Certificates # Create client certificates for remote users cockroach cert create-client appuser --certs-dir=certs --ca-key=ca-key/ca.key cockroach cert create-client backupuser --certs-dir=certs --ca-key=ca- key/ca.key cockroach cert create-client monitoruser --certs-dir=certs --ca-key=ca- key/ca.key # Securely distribute certificates to remote hosts # Application server scp certs/ca.crt certs/client.appuser.* appserver:/var/lib/cockroach/certs/ ssh appserver "chown -R app:app /var/lib/cockroach/certs && chmod 600 /var/lib/cockroach/certs/client.appuser.key" # Backup server scp certs/ca.crt certs/client.backupuser.* backupserver:/opt/backup/certs/ ssh backupserver "chown -R backup:backup /opt/backup/certs && chmod 600 /opt/backup/certs/client.backupuser.key" # Monitoring server scp certs/ca.crt certs/client.monitoruser.* monitor:/var/lib/monitoring/certs/ ssh monitor "chown -R monitor:monitor /var/lib/monitoring/certs && chmod 600 /var/lib/monitoring/certs/client.monitoruser.key" 4. Network Security Configuration # Configure firewall to restrict access (example with iptables) # Allow only specific hosts to connect to CockroachDB port iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 26257 -s 10.0.1.100 -j ACCEPT # app server iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 26257 -s 10.0.1.200 -j ACCEPT # backup server iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 26257 -s 10.0.1.300 -j ACCEPT # monitor server iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 26257 -j DROP # deny all others # For cloud environments, use security groups or network policies # Example AWS security group rule: # Port: 26257, Protocol: TCP, Source: sg-app-servers # Port: 26257, Protocol: TCP, Source: sg-backup-servers 5. Test Remote Connectivity # Test from application server ssh appserver cockroach sql --certs-dir=/var/lib/cockroach/certs --host=database- server:26257 --user=appuser # Test from backup server ssh backupserver cockroach sql --certs-dir=/opt/backup/certs --host=database-server:26257 -- user=backupuser # Test connection pooling and load balancing cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs -- host=db1.example.com:26257,db2.example.com:26257,db3.example.com:26257 -- user=appuser

check.check-content: Prerequisites: Ensure certificate infrastructure is properly configured (see section 6.0). Test certificate-based authentication for remote connections: # Test from remote host using certificates cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=database-server:26257 --user=root root@database-server:26257/defaultdb> Verify TLS encryption is enforced: # Attempt insecure connection (should fail) cockroach sql --insecure --host=database-server:26257 --user=root ERROR: server is not running in insecure mode, must use certificates # Test secure connection cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=database-server:26257 --user=root root@database-server:26257/defaultdb> Test password-based authentication over TLS: # First, set password for user (if using password auth) cockroach sql --certs-dir=certs --host=database-server:26257 --execute="ALTER USER appuser WITH PASSWORD 'secure_password';" # Test password authentication from remote host cockroach sql --host=database-server:26257 --user=appuser Enter password: appuser@database-server:26257/defaultdb> Verify connection from multiple remote locations: # Test from application server cockroach sql --certs-dir=app-certs --host=db1.example.com:26257 -- user=appuser # Test from backup server cockroach sql --certs-dir=backup-certs --host=db1.example.com:26257 -- user=backupuser # Test from monitoring system cockroach sql --certs-dir=monitor-certs --host=db1.example.com:26257 -- user=monitoruser Check TLS configuration and cipher suites: # Verify TLS version and cipher suites (requires openssl) echo | openssl s_client -connect database-server:26257 -tls1_2 2>/dev/null | grep -E "(Protocol|Cipher)"

Rule.title: Ensure Security Audit Logging Is Enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB provides comprehensive audit logging capabilities to track security- relevant events including user authentication, privilege changes, and access to sensitive data. Role-based audit logging allows administrators to configure which users, roles, or statements should be logged, while sensitive access logging can track access to specific tables or databases containing sensitive information. Audit logging is essential for compliance, security monitoring, incident response, and detecting unauthorized access or privilege escalation attempts. CockroachDB supports multiple logging channels including SESSIONS, USER_ADMIN, PRIVILEGES, and SENSITIVE_ACCESS that can be configured to capture different types of security events. The sql.log.user_audit cluster setting enables role-based audit logging, allowing administrators to specify which users or roles should have their SQL statements logged. Additionally, table-level audit logging can be enabled using EXPERIMENTAL_AUDIT to track all access (read and write) to sensitive tables.
Rationale: Security audit logging provides several critical functions: • Accountability: Establishes a record of who performed what actions and when, supporting non-repudiation requirements • Compliance: Many regulatory frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOX, GDPR) require audit trails for sensitive data access • Threat Detection: Enables detection of suspicious patterns, unauthorized access attempts, or privilege escalation • Incident Response: Provides forensic evidence for security incidents and data breaches • Operational Monitoring: Helps identify misconfigurations, policy violations, or operational issues Without proper audit logging, organizations cannot effectively monitor database activity, detect security incidents, or demonstrate compliance with regulatory requirements. Logging should capture authentication events, privilege changes, and access to sensitive data as a minimum baseline for Level 1 security.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Enable role-based SQL audit logging:: Enable role-based SQL audit logging Configure sql.log.user_audit with appropriate rules. The setting uses a table-like syntax where each row specifies a user/role and a statement filter ( ALL or NONE). Example - audit all statements for all users: -- Example - audit all statements for all users: SET CLUSTER SETTING sql.log.user_audit = 'ALL ALL';; -- Example - audit all statements for specific roles (one per line): SET CLUSTER SETTING sql.log.user_audit = ' admin ALL root ALL '; (Adjust syntax to match your CockroachDB version's documented examples.) 2. Configure security logging channels in an auditable sink: Ensure your logging configuration includes a security file group with the recommended channels and auditable: true: sinks: file-groups: security: channels: [SESSIONS, USER_ADMIN, PRIVILEGES, SENSITIVE_ACCESS] auditable: true Apply the configuration according to your deployment method (for example, via log- config at node start or the appropriate cluster setting, depending on version). 3. Enable connection/authentication logging: Turn on SQL client connection logging to the SESSIONS channel: SET CLUSTER SETTING server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled = true; 4. (Optional) Optimize audit evaluation performance: If you use complex sql.log.user_audit configurations, consider enabling reduced-config evaluation to compute the audit configuration once per session: SET CLUSTER SETTING sql.log.user_audit.reduced_config.enabled = true;

check.check-content: 1. Verify role-based audit logging is configured: SHOW CLUSTER SETTING sql.log.user_audit; • The documented syntax for sql.log.user_audit is table-like text, where each line is: USER_OR_ROLE STATEMENT_FILTER This setting must contain one or more audit rules in the documented table-like syntax (user/role and statement filter). Expected Results (conceptual): • sql.log.user_audit is non-empty and includes appropriate entries for privileged users/roles (for example, admin, root, or an equivalent privileged role), or a global rule (for example, ALL). o Explicit entries for privileged users/roles (for example, admin ALL, root ALL, or other high-privilege roles). 2. Check logging channel configuration: Review the logging configuration to ensure a file sink (for example, security) includes the security-relevant channels and is marked auditable. A typical configuration is: sinks: file-groups: security: channels: [SESSIONS, USER_ADMIN, PRIVILEGES, SENSITIVE_ACCESS] auditable: true This writes combined output to a cockroach-security.log file in the configured logging directory and enforces non-repudiable logging via auditable: true. Expected Results: A sink exists that includes SESSIONS, USER_ADMIN, PRIVILEGES, and SENSITIVE_ACCESS, and auditable: true is set for that sink. Fail if: • These channels are not present in any sink, or • No security-relevant sink is configured as auditable. 3. Verify security event logging is active: For connection events, confirm the cluster setting is enabled: SHOW CLUSTER SETTING server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled; Expected Results: • server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled is true, and • The SESSIONS channel is included in an active sink. Fail if: • server.auth_log.sql_connections.enabled is false or • SESSIONS is not routed to any sink. 4. Test audit log generation: As a privileged user covered by sql.log.user_audit, execute a simple statement (for example, a SELECT or CREATE USER) and verify that an audit event is written to the configured sink (for example, cockroach-security.log). Expected Results: • The test statement appears in the audit logs with timestamp, user, and statement text. Fail if: • No corresponding audit entry is observed in the configured logs.

Rule.title: Ensure OCSP Certificate Revocation Checking Is Enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) is a mechanism for checking whether a certificate has been revoked by its Certificate Authority (CA) before it expires. CockroachDB supports OCSP checking through the security.ocsp.mode cluster setting, which can be configured to verify certificate revocation status when validating client and node certificates. When enabled, CockroachDB will query the OCSP responder specified in the certificate (or a configured OCSP server) to verify that certificates have not been revoked. This provides defense-in-depth for certificate-based authentication by ensuring that compromised or revoked certificates cannot be used to authenticate to the cluster, even if they are still within their validity period. OCSP checking is particularly important in environments where certificates may need to be revoked before expiration due to: • Compromised private keys • Certificate misuse or unauthorized access • Organizational policy changes • Employee termination or role changes
Rationale: Certificate revocation checking addresses a critical gap in certificate-based authentication: a certificate that is valid (not expired) but has been revoked should not be accepted for authentication. Without OCSP checking, a compromised certificate could continue to be used until it naturally expires, which could be months or years.
