Key security benefits of OCSP checking include: • Revocation Detection: Immediately detects and rejects certificates that have been revoked by the CA • Compromise Response: Enables rapid response to certificate compromises by revoking affected certificates • Compliance: Meets requirements for certificate validation in regulated environments • Defense-in-Depth: Adds an additional layer of security beyond basic certificate validation The security.ocsp.mode setting supports three modes: • off: OCSP checking is disabled (default) • lax: OCSP checking is performed, but certificate validation succeeds even if OCSP check fails (e.g., OCSP server unavailable) • strict: OCSP checking is required, and certificate validation fails if OCSP check fails or cannot be performed For production environments, strict mode is recommended to ensure that revoked certificates are always rejected, though lax mode may be appropriate in environments where OCSP server availability cannot be guaranteed.</VulnDiscussion>
Rule.fixtext: 1. Enable OCSP checking: Configure OCSP mode based on organizational requirements: -- For production with reliable OCSP server: use strict mode SET CLUSTER SETTING security.ocsp.mode = 'strict'; -- For environments where OCSP server availability cannot be guaranteed: use lax mode SET CLUSTER SETTING security.ocsp.mode = 'lax'; Mode Selection: • strict: Recommended for production. Certificates will be rejected if OCSP check fails or cannot be performed. Requires reliable OCSP server availability. • lax: Use when OCSP server availability cannot be guaranteed. Certificates are validated even if OCSP check fails, but revoked certificates are still rejected when OCSP check succeeds. 2. Configure OCSP cache and timeout (if needed): Optimize OCSP performance and reliability: -- Configure OCSP query timeout (default: 3s) SET CLUSTER SETTING security.ocsp.timeout = '5s'; Recommended Values: • Timeout: 3s to 10s (prevent blocking certificate validation) 3. Ensure certificates include OCSP responder URLs: When generating certificates, ensure they include OCSP responder information: ## When creating certificates, include OCSP responder URL in certificate extensions # This is typically handled by the CA or certificate generation tool cockroach cert create-client \ client_name \ --certs-dir=certs \ --ca-key=ca-key/ca.key \ --ocsp-url=https://ocsp.example.com 4. Certificate Validation # Verify certificate chain openssl verify -CAfile certs/ca.crt certs/node.crt # Check certificate expiration dates for cert in certs/*.crt; do echo "Certificate: $cert" openssl x509 -in "$cert" -noout -dates echo done Note: OCSP responder URLs can be specified in certificates or configured separately depending on the certificate generation method used. 5. Verify OCSP server availability: Ensure OCSP responder is accessible and functioning: # Test OCSP responder accessibility curl -I https://ocsp.example.com # Test OCSP query openssl ocsp -issuer certs/ca.crt -cert certs/client.crt \ -url https://ocsp.example.com 6. Monitor OCSP checking: After enabling OCSP, monitor for: • OCSP query failures or timeouts • Certificate validation failures due to OCSP issues • Performance impact from OCSP checking -- Monitor certificate validation (may require log analysis) -- Check for OCSP-related errors in logs 7. Document OCSP configuration: Maintain documentation of: • OCSP mode selection and rationale • OCSP server locations and availability requirements • Cache and timeout settings • Procedures for certificate revocation • Monitoring and alerting for OCSP failures

check.check-content: 1. Verify OCSP mode is configured: SHOW CLUSTER SETTING security.ocsp.mode; Expected Results: • Should be set to strict or lax (not off) • strict is recommended for production environments with reliable OCSP server availability • lax may be acceptable if OCSP server availability cannot be guaranteed Fail if: • The setting is off (disabled) • The setting is not configured (defaults to off) 2. Verify OCSP server configuration (if applicable): Check if OCSP servers are configured for certificate validation: -- Check cluster settings related to OCSP SHOW CLUSTER SETTING security.ocsp.timeout; Expected Results: • OCSP timeout settings should be configured appropriately if OCSP is enabled • Timeout should be reasonable (e.g., 3s to 10s) to avoid blocking certificate validation Note: Some OCSP configuration may be specified in certificates themselves (OCSP responder URLs) rather than cluster settings. 3. Test OCSP checking behavior: To verify OCSP checking is working: # Check certificate for OCSP responder URL openssl x509 -in certs/client.crt -noout -ocsp_uri # Test OCSP query (if OCSP responder is accessible) openssl ocsp -issuer certs/ca.crt -cert certs/client.crt \ -url $(openssl x509 -in certs/client.crt -noout -ocsp_uri) Expected Results: • Certificates should include OCSP responder URLs (if OCSP is to be used) • OCSP queries should return valid responses when certificates are not revoked 4. Review certificate validation logs: Check logs for OCSP-related messages: # Check for OCSP validation in logs grep -i "ocsp" /var/lib/cockroach/logs/cockroach.log | tail -20 Expected Results: • Logs should show OCSP checking activity when certificates are validated • No errors indicating OCSP server unavailability (if in strict mode)

Rule.title: Ensure SQL Session Idle Timeouts Are Configured for SQL Roles
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>CockroachDB allows administrators to define role-level SQL session idle timeouts using the idle_in_session_timeout session variable. This setting ensures that any session authenticated under a given SQL role is automatically terminated after a defined period of inactivity. Configuring idle session timeouts for SQL roles provides a more granular control model than cluster-wide settings. It ensures that different classes of users — such as read-only roles, application service accounts, or privileged administrators — are governed by timeout values that reflect their risk level and organizational policy. This control is particularly important for organizations subject to compliance frameworks that mandate automatic termination of inactive sessions (e.g., SOC 2, NIST 800-53 AC-12, PCI DSS 8.2.8). Using per-role idle session timeouts helps enforce consistent and auditable policy compliance.
Rationale: Without enforced role-level idle timeout settings, SQL sessions may remain active indefinitely, creating several risks: Security Risks • Abandoned Session Exposure: Idle but authenticated sessions can be abused if an attacker gains access to the client environment or connection path. • Privilege Abuse: Privileged roles without idle timeouts increase the likelihood of misuse or lateral movement. • Session Hijacking: Long-lived sessions expand the window of opportunity for an attacker to intercept and reuse session credentials. Compliance Risks Many standards require automatic termination of inactive sessions. For example: • SOC 2 (CC6.x): Requires controls on session management. • NIST 800-53 AC-12: Requires automatic session termination after inactivity. • PCI DSS 8.2.8: Requires session timeouts of 15 minutes or less unless justified. Failure to configure role-specific idle timeouts may lead to audit findings and non- compliance. Operational Benefits • Reduces buildup of idle or abandoned sessions • Provides predictable resource usage • Enforces security baselines consistently across user groups</VulnDiscussion>

Set idle timeout for a SQL role: Set a reasonable timeout for idle connections: ALTER ROLE <role_name> SET idle_in_session_timeout = '<duration>'; -- Example - set 30-minute idle timeout for a read-only role: ALTER ROLE table_reader SET idle_in_session_timeout = '30m'; Recommended Values • High-security environments: 10m-15m • Standard enterprise roles: 15m-30m • Administrative roles: 15m-30m (stricter values recommended) • Application roles: 30m-1h (with documented justification) Values should reflect: • Organizational security policies • Compliance requirements • Justified business or application needs 2. Verify timeout configuration after applying settings: SHOW DEFAULT SESSION VARIABLES FOR ROLE <role_name>; Expected Results: • idle_in_session_timeout reflects the newly configured value. Note on Session Variable Precedence: idle_in_session_timeout will use the newly configured default, but CockroachDB applies session variables according to a precedence hierarchy. Even if you set idle_in_session_timeout globally (for example with ALTER ROLE ALL SET idle_in_session_timeout = { value } or at a role level), a user can: • Override it in their current session with SET idle_in_session_timeout = { value }, and • Have it overridden by a more specific ALTER ROLE { role_name } IN DATABASE { db_name } SET idle_in_session_timeout = { value } setting, which takes precedence over broader role- or cluster-level defaults. 3. Document configuration: Maintain documentation that includes: • Assigned timeout values per role • Rationale supporting each timeout (e.g., compliance mapping) • Exceptions or deviations • Review process and periodic re-validation
